Bind SkyRPG enchants at the Arcane Enchanting screen, use tomes, combine and salvage them, and fill the Codex.

SkyRPG replaces vanilla's enchanting table with its own enchants: 72 of them, from simple stat boosts to effects like lightning and cheating death. You bind them at Arcane Enchanting, find them as tomes, and every bind levels the Enchanting skill. This page covers how it all works. The full enchant list is on Enchant list. Vanilla enchanted books from loot and the anvil still work as before.

Seraphine Vael, the Enchanter in the tower in the hub. Her library counts as 15 bookshelves, and you can stay within 12 blocks of her.
Any enchanting table. Right-click it to open the same screen. Stay within 8 blocks of the table.
A table's power is the number of bookshelves around it (vanilla's rule: two blocks out, with air between), up to 15. Higher enchant levels need power:
A table only offers up to level V. Higher levels (some enchants go to VI or VII) only come from tomes.
A violet window with an altar in the middle: two rune rings turn against each other and light bursts when something is bound. It has three tabs.

Enchant: your enchantable gear on the left (worn armour first, then the held item, hotbar, bag and offhand), the item on the altar with what it already holds, and the enchants the table offers for it on the right. Pick an enchant and a level, then Bind. Locked levels say why (bookshelves, or your Enchanting level).
Tomes: your tomes on the left. For the chosen tome you can Combine it with an identical one, Salvage it into Runic Dust, or Apply it to any item you carry that takes it. Each row shows the change, for example "II to Keen III", and the cost.
Codex: every enchant there is, filtered by weapons, bows, armour, tools, fishing and ultimates, with what each does at its highest level and where it comes from. Hover for every level and the conflicts. Tome-only enchants you have not seen yet show as runes.
Replacing something (a conflicting enchant, or another ultimate) needs a second click. The footer shows your coins, XP levels, Lapis, Runic Dust and Enchanting level.

Each enchant goes on a kind of item: swords, bows and crossbows, armour (any piece or one slot), pickaxes, axes, hoes, any tool, fishing rods or wands. Only single items can be enchanted, never a stack. Armour enchants work in their own slot, and everything else works while held in your main hand. An item with enchants glints.

Conflicts: Keen, Hallowed Edge and Webcutter exclude each other.
Ultimates: an item holds only one ultimate.
An enchant costs coins, XP levels, Lapis and, for the rarer ones, Runic Dust and Prism Fragments. Each level is paid in full, not as a difference. Materials are taken from your backpacks too.
Reseeding has its own price (4,000 coins, 8 XP levels, Enchanting 5, 12 Lapis and 16 Dewdrops).
A tome is an item that holds one enchant at one level. Apply it at the screen to put that enchant on an item.

Applying gives the tome's level if it is higher than the item's. A tome of the same level as the item's raises it by one, up to the enchant's maximum. It costs coins (300 for Common up to 25,000 for an Ultimate, times the level it ends at) and 3 XP levels per level.
Combining two identical tomes (same enchant, same level) makes one a level higher. This is the only way past the table's level V. It costs coins (150 to 10,000 times the new level squared) and, from Uncommon up, Runic Dust.
Salvaging a tome gives Runic Dust: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 or 40 by rarity (Common to Ultimate), doubled for every level above I. Runic Dust sells for 80 coins, but the best binds and merges ask for it.

Hostile mobs: about 0.5% per kill, a little more for tougher mobs (up to 2%), times Magic Find and the Tome Hunter talent. They are combat enchants of levels I to III, mostly Common. Spawner mobs never drop them.
Gathering: while you gain XP in a skill, there is a small chance of a tome for that skill's gear: mining 0.06%, foraging 0.06%, farming 0.04%, fishing 1% per catch. The skill's ultimate is much rarer (mining and foraging 0.003%, farming 0.002%, fishing 0.06%).
Slayer bosses and the world boss: each drops its own enchants (and a small chance of Unbreakable), with a higher tier giving better odds.
Dungeon bosses and champions: each dungeon boss and champion has its own tome drops.

SkyRPG's gathering tools (pickaxes, axes, hoes and scythes, and fishing rods) wear down and must be repaired (see Tools). Unbreakable is a single-level Legendary enchant that goes on any of them and makes the tool take no durability damage at all. It does not repair a tool that is already worn.

It does nothing on weapons, armour, shields, bows or accessories, which never wear in the first place.

The Artisan Bench, how recipes unlock, the gear ladders, tool tiers and which blocks pay out.

Almost all SkyRPG gear is crafted at the Artisan Bench. Unlike the vanilla crafting grid, it asks for exact counts ("32 Skyiron Ingots"), locks recipes behind skill levels, and takes the old item as an ingredient so upgrades keep their enchantments. This page covers the bench, the gear ladders it builds, tool tiers and the placed-block rules.
Artisan Bench is a block you can place anywhere. Get one by:

Crafting it at a crafting table: a crafting table in the middle, 4 iron ingots on the edges and 4 Glimmer Crystals in the corners.
Buying one from Dorrin Saltmarsh at Saltmarsh Provisions for 1,500 coins.
Right-click it to open the crafting screen. Admins can open it anywhere with /bench, and NPCs can open it too.
Before you have your own, use the public bench in Skyhaven: it stands in the Emberforge yard, next to Brannoc Ashforge (by the smithing table). It's the only bench you can use in the hub.

Left: categories. One for each kind of recipe (backpacks, combat, cooking, dungeon, farming, fishing, foraging, mining, region and slayer), with ★ Pinned, ✔ Ready to craft (everything you can make right now) and All on top. While you track a recipe there is also a ◆ Tracked tab, and the bench opens on it with that recipe selected. Each shows how many recipes it has, in green when one of them is ready. On a small window only the icons show; hover one for its name.
Middle: the recipes, grouped under Weapons, Tools, Armour, Accessories, Backpacks and Materials, with the ones you can make first. The chip on the right of each row says where you stand: ✔ 3 (you can craft it 3 times), 1/2 (you have enough of 1 of its 2 ingredients) or ✖ Mining 18 (still locked). A ★ marks a pinned recipe and a ◆ the tracked one.
Right: the selected recipe. The result, big (hover it for its full tooltip), what it needs, and every ingredient with how many you have of how many you need and a bar. Under it are four buttons: Craft, Craft ×N (as many as you can afford, up to 64), ★ Pin and ◆ Track.

Click a recipe to select it, double-click to craft one, Shift+double-click to craft as many as you can.
↑ / ↓ move the selection, Enter crafts one and Shift+Enter as many as you can.
P pins or unpins the selected recipe. Pinned recipes are kept on your computer and the bench opens on the Pinned tab when you have any.
The search box at the top right finds recipes in every category by the name of the result or of any ingredient. Click it (or press Ctrl+F) and type; Enter or Esc leaves it.
Right-click a recipe (or press T) to track it. A box on the right of your screen then lists its ingredients with how many you have of how many you need (backpacks count), updated every second, and says when it's ready to craft (or what it still needs to unlock). Do it again to stop. The box can be moved or hidden in the HUD editor ("Tracked Recipe").
With JEI (part of the pack), every bench recipe also shows in JEI's "Artisan Bench" tab: press R on an item for its recipes or U for what it's used in.
Ingredients come from your inventory and from inside your carried backpacks.
Recipes unlock as your skill levels rise, and the level-up message lists the new ones ("NEW RECIPES at the Artisan Bench").

Most gear recipes take the previous piece as their first ingredient. The result keeps the old item's custom name, enchantments, lore and contents, so a backpack keeps what is inside it and a pickaxe keeps its Prosperity (SkyRPG enchants and all). The new tool comes fully repaired, so upgrading also mends a worn one. Only SkyRPG tools, armour, accessories and backpacks count as the item being upgraded.
A handful of recipes also need a collection tier (see Collections). The recipe shows "Requires Skyiron Collection III" while it is locked.
Some things stay at the normal crafting table and show in the recipe book (each item's wiki page draws its 3x3 grid):

The Artisan Bench, the Satchel (string, leather and an iron ingot) and the starter gear: the Prospector set and pickaxe (stone, iron), the Harvester set and hoe (hay blocks), the Woodsman set and axe (logs) and the Vanguard set (iron and redstone blocks). Armour sets has the details.
Compacting: 9 Glimmer Shards make a Glimmer Crystal, 9 Dewdrops a Dew Vial, 9 Tidescales a Tidescale Plate, 9 Heartwood Splinters a Heartwood Bundle, 9 Valor Marks a Valor Seal, and each reverses. Skyiron Ingots, Emberite Ingots and Duskquartz Shards pack into blocks.
Smelting: Raw Skyiron in a furnace or blast furnace, Emberite Chunks and Hellforged Scrap in a blast furnace only.
Planks of the five new woods, which work in every vanilla wood recipe.

Each skill has a ladder of gear. You make each step from the one before it, and every step is unlocked by a skill level and the material of that tier. The ladders follow a rough pattern (the exact levels are in the next table):

Details for each skill's recipes are on its page: Mining, Farming, Foraging and Fishing. Combat gear is on Weapons and Armour sets, and backpacks are on Backpacks.

Combat recipes are paid in Valor Marks and Valor Seals (nine Marks make a Seal), with Dread Fangs and Nightmare Cores from monsters as the rare ingredient. The Fangguard set and Fangsteel Sabre need Combat 10, Stormedge and Stormplate 18, Riftblade and Riftweave 26, Cinderfang and Cinderguard 35, and Starfall Blade and Starforged 45.
Three more groups of recipes use their own unlocks:

Dungeon recipes need Delving levels and boss tokens (Warden Sigils, Arachne Eyes, Tide Pearls, Dwarven Cogs and so on). See Delving.
Slayer recipes need a slayer level for that boss and its tokens. Each piece of a set unlocks at a different slayer level (boots at 2, helmet at 4, leggings at 5, chestplate at 7, and the weapon at 6). See Slayers.
Region recipes need Combat levels and the essences from a danger region's monsters. See Danger regions.

Pickaxes and axes have a tier from I to VII, and SkyRPG's tougher ores and woods need a minimum tier. A block that needs a higher tier does not crack at all, and the action bar and look-at box say what you need.
II | Stone, copper | Quarry Pick, Woodsman Axe
III | Iron | Prospector and Delver's Pickaxes
IV | Diamond | Skyiron Pickaxe, Ironbark Hatchet
V | Netherite | Duskbore Pick, Mistpine Splitter
VI | None | Emberheart and Hellforged Pickaxes, Willowcleaver
VII | None | Lumen Breaker, Emberbrand Axe, Starwood Greataxe
Mining gates: Skyiron needs II, Duskquartz IV, Emberite and Hellforged V, Lumenite VI. Foraging gates: Ironbark III, Mistpine IV, Duskwillow V, Emberwood VI, Starwood VII. See Tools for every tool.

You cannot farm XP by placing blocks and breaking them again. The game remembers every block a player places, and a placed block gives no skill XP, no Glimmer Shards, no rare finds, no event points and no contract progress when broken.

Some things pay out even when you place them, because placing them is how you use them: crops and saplings, sugar cane, cactus, cocoa, nether wart, bamboo, sweet berry bushes, melon and pumpkin stems, kelp, mushrooms, mining nodes, foraging stumps and planters. (A melon or pumpkin block you placed still gives nothing.) Treefeller also never fells logs you placed.

Nodes, stumps and planters are the safe way to get a steady income of Glimmer, Heartwood and Dew while you are away from the big world. They are cheaper XP than ores, so mix them with real mining, chopping and farming.

The dungeon skill: how Delving XP is earned, what each level gives and which gear it unlocks.

Delving is the skill of exploring dungeons. You earn Delving XP from opening dungeon chests, finding secrets, slaying champions and bosses, and discovering dungeons. Its levels give Health and Magic Find, and unlock the dungeon recipes at the Artisan Bench. Level 50 is the cap, on the same curve as the other skills (see Skills overview).

+2 Health and +0.25 Magic Find.
One talent point for the Delving talents.
Every 5th level pays coins (level x 100).
Unlocks for bench recipes (see below).
Delving Insight adds 1% Delving XP per point. It comes from the Delver set and Delver Pickaxe and the Scholar's Focus helmet enchant.
Discovering a dungeon (walking up to its entrance, once) | 100 plus 5 per dungeon level
Opening a dungeon chest | Chest rate times the dungeon level (table below)
Slaying a champion | 400 to 6,000, by dungeon
Slaying a boss | 1,500 to 28,000, by dungeon
Every chest is per player: each of you rolls your own loot and gets your own coins and XP, and the chest refills when the dungeon resets. The XP of a chest is the dungeon's level times its rate:
Coins vary by 20% either way. A vault in the Forgotten Crypt (dungeon level 12) pays about 1,200 coins and 300 XP.
Every boss and champion pays Delving XP to everyone who took part in the kill, on every kill.

Minions work a block for you while you're away and keep half the skill XP for you.

A Minion works one block for you: every 30 seconds it mines its ore, chops its log or harvests its crop, and keeps the drops and half the skill XP until you collect them. It keeps working while you are away or offline (the server only has to be running) and holds up to 2 hours of work (240 actions). After that it stops and puffs angry clouds until you empty it.
Craft it at the Artisan Bench (Minions tab): 2 Iron Blocks, 32 Redstone, 16 Copper Ingots and 8 Amethyst Shards. No skill level is needed.
You can have one minion, plus one more per 10 levels of your best skill, so six at level 50.

Place it anywhere in the survival world.
Right-click it with the block it should work: an ore (Iron Ore, Diamond Ore...), a log, or seeds for a crop (Wheat Seeds, a Carrot, a Potato...). Anything that gives skill XP when you break it works. It shows little puffs of that block while it works.
Right-click it with an empty hand (or anything else) to collect: the items go into your inventory (or drop at your feet if it's full) and you get the XP. Chat shows what it made.
Right-click it with a different block to change its work; it hands over what it made first.
Only the owner can collect from a minion or break it. Breaking it collects everything first and gives the Minion back.
Speed | one action every 30 seconds (120 an hour)
XP | half of what breaking the block yourself gives; Insight does not boost it, an XP boost (like a 2x weekend) running when you collect does
Drops | the block's normal drops, without Fortune

The sword lines, region, dungeon and slayer weapons, the Mending Wand and how weapon abilities work.

Weapons are what you hit monsters with. SkyRPG's weapons are not drops you hope for: almost all of them are crafted at the Artisan Bench from monster drops, boss tokens and the previous weapon in their line. Each line has a clear path, and the better weapons carry abilities and special effects.
A weapon's Damage is its base damage before anything else. Your stats then change it:

Strength adds 1% to your melee damage per point. A weapon with 20 Strength is 20% stronger, and the Strength on your armour and talents stacks with it.
Crit Chance is the chance for a hit to be a critical hit (you start with 30%). A crit multiplies the hit by 1 + Crit Damage / 100 (you start with 50% Crit Damage).
Defense on a target cuts damage the same way, so 100 Defense halves it.

Weapons also carry set effects and perks. "Heals 3% of the damage you deal" is life steal, "+40% damage to spiders" is a bane effect that only counts against that kind of mob, and "poison" or "sets on fire" apply to what you hit. See Stats and Combat basics for the full picture.
Some weapons have an ability you use with right-click. There are two kinds:

Cooldown abilities are free but have a cooldown (tools such as the Treefeller axes and Skyward Burst).
Mana abilities cost mana and have a cooldown too. Your mana is 100 plus 1 per point of Intelligence (Starfall costs 50, Thunderclap 30, Riftstep 50, Void Rend 80, the Mending Wand's Mend 60).

Every ability announces itself with effects and sound, and the item shows its recharge as a dark sweep over its hotbar slot. If you try too early, or without enough mana, the action bar tells you why (in red, with a dull click) and nothing is spent. A long recharge ends with a chime and a green "ready" message while you hold the item. The big ones also give your screen a short shake, so you feel them land.

Starfall (Starfall Blade): a ring of stars opens under you and a target ring closes on every hostile mob within 6 blocks (up to 14). A star then falls out of the sky onto each one, nearest first, a star every tenth of a second, and every star lands with a flash, a ring, a burst of sparks and a bell note that climbs with each one. Each does 80 damage and flings the mob into the air. Three or more stars end with a bloom of light across the whole field.
Thunderclap (Stormedge): a blue shockwave rolls out of you, then lightning hits every hostile mob within 5 blocks (up to 12), nearest first, with a spark arcing from each to the next. Each takes 40 damage and is shocked (slowed hard) for 1.5 seconds.
Void Rend (Voidreaver): a violet rift opens 3 to 4 blocks ahead of you and spins, and for 0.7 seconds it drags every hostile mob within 8 blocks (up to 16) towards it. Bosses and heavy mobs resist in proportion to their knockback resistance. Then the rift collapses with a shockwave, a flash and a thunderclap of sound: each mob takes 150 damage and Wither II for 3 seconds and is shoved outwards. Nothing is spent if there is nothing to rend.
Riftstep (Riftblade): you tear through the air up to 8 blocks and leave a violet cut hanging along the path. Every hostile mob the cut touches takes 40 damage. It stops short of walls and costs nothing if a wall is in the way.

The main sword ladder is paid in Valor Marks (dropped by levelled mobs, more often the higher their level, nine make a Valor Seal) and rare drops from monsters. Each sword is made from the one before it and keeps its name and enchantments. Combat gear unlocks at Combat 10, 18, 26, 35, 45 and 50.

The Mending Wand is a wand, not a sword. It has 50 Intelligence and the ability Mend (right-click): it costs 60 mana and heals you for 40 health, with a 5 second cooldown, in a spiral of green and gold light. At full health it does nothing and costs nothing. Odessa Quill sells it at Quill's Curiosities for 18,000 coins. The Spellweave enchant (+55 Intelligence while held) goes on wands.

Enchants are the main way to improve a weapon beyond its base numbers (see Enchanting). Sword enchants include Keen (+40% damage at the top level), Hallowed Edge and Webcutter (more damage to the undead and to spiders), Bloodthirst (life steal), Frostbite, Venom Coat, Cleave (hits nearby enemies), Reaper's Mark, Titanbane and the ultimates Soulrend and Rift Echo. Bow enchants such as Deadeye, Splitshot and Starshot work with the vanilla bows and crossbows that Kestrel Vane sells.

The strongest weapons and tools are drawn with larger, animated art (sheens, lightning, embers, stars, runes) and the biggest blades are held larger. Turn this on or off in Settings, Interface, Detailed weapon art. Some weapons also show held particles around the hand (Settings, Gameplay, Weapon particles).

Every armour set, its full-set bonus and where it comes from, grouped by skill, combat, slayer, dungeon and region, with 3D looks.

SkyRPG armour comes in sets of four pieces (helmet, chestplate, leggings and boots). Each piece gives its own stats, and wearing all four adds a full-set bonus: extra stats plus an effect that does something you can feel, such as Night Vision underground or lightning-fast replanting. There are 42 sets, from starter gear you craft at a table to legendary sets from bosses.

Wear all four pieces of the same set for the bonus. Fewer pieces give the piece stats only.
Piece stats and the set's bonus stats are added to your stats, so they show up on the Stats page (see Stats).
SkyRPG armour does not break.
Most sets are made at the Artisan Bench from materials, not from the previous set. Armour enchants count in their slot (see Enchanting).
Names in the tables: "Four pieces together" adds up the stats of the helmet, chestplate, leggings and boots. The bonus stats are on top of that. Rarity is the rarity of the chestplate (the slayer sets have Epic helmets, leggings and boots with a Legendary chestplate).
The cards under each table show a chestplate from each set. The other three pieces are in Items: armour.
Pieces of different sets still add their own stats. If you cannot afford a full set yet, mix pieces for the stats you need, then complete one set later for the bonus.

Each gathering skill has a ladder of sets. The first is a starter you can buy or craft from vanilla materials. The rest unlock at Skill levels 8 to 45, and are made from the previous tier's materials. Each full-set bonus is tied to its skill.

Stats
Every pickaxe, axe, hoe, scythe and fishing rod with its tier, stats, ability and how to make it.

Tools are how you gather. SkyRPG has a ladder of pickaxes, axes, hoes and scythes, and fishing rods, each made at the Artisan Bench from the one before it. Tools carry gathering stats (Mining Speed, Fortune, Fishing Speed...) that apply while you hold them, and the better ones have a right-click ability. Tools wear down as you use them, but a SkyRPG tool never disappears: at 1 durability it is broken until you repair it (see Durability and repair below).

Stats while held. A pickaxe's Mining Speed and Mining Fortune only count while it is in your hand. Gathering stats from armour, talents and enchants add on top.
Tiers. Pickaxes and axes have a tier from I to VII. SkyRPG's harder ores and woods need a minimum tier, and a weaker tool does not crack them at all (see Crafting).
Abilities. The better tools have a right-click ability with a cooldown. They do not cost mana.
Upgrades keep your enchants. The bench keeps a tool's name and enchantments when you upgrade it.
Enchants. Pickaxes, axes, hoes (scythes count as hoes), any tool and fishing rods each take their own kind of enchant (see Enchanting).

Every pickaxe, axe, hoe, scythe and fishing rod has a durability that grows with its tier, so the tools you use most last longest. Weapons, armour, shields, bows, wands, backpacks and accessories do not wear: they stay unbreakable.
Quarry Pick, Woodsman Axe, Harvester Hoe | 250
For comparison, vanilla's wooden tools have 59, iron 250, diamond 1,561 and netherite 2,031. The tooltip and the bar under the item show what is left.

A pickaxe or axe loses 1 durability for each block it breaks. A hoe or scythe loses 1 for each ripe crop you harvest (and when it tills soil). A rod loses 1 each time you reel in.
Big abilities are cheap. The extra blocks broken by Treefeller, the scythes' 3x3 and 5x5 sweeps and the extra ore of a Veinseeker or Hellfire Vein cost only 1 durability per 4 extra blocks, so felling a whole tree costs a few points, not thirty.
Creative mode never wears a tool.

Broken tools. A SkyRPG tool never breaks for good. When it would, it stays at 1 durability and the action bar says "Your tool is broken, repair it". A broken tool mines at hand speed, drops nothing that needs a tool, counts as no tier, gives none of its stats, perks or enchants, cannot use its ability and cannot till, strip or cast, until it is repaired. Treefeller and sweeps stop when the tool runs out.

Anvil with the tool's own material. Put the tool and its material in an anvil; each piece restores a quarter of its durability, as in vanilla. Iron-tier tools (Quarry Pick, Delver's Pickaxe, Woodsman Axe, Ironbark Hatchet, Harvester Hoe, Thornfield Sickle, Sunreaper Scythe) take iron ingots, diamond-tier tools (Prospector, Skyiron, Duskbore and Emberheart Pickaxes, Mistpine Splitter, Willowcleaver, Frostbite and Cinder Scythes) take diamonds, and netherite-tier tools (Hellforged Pickaxe, Lumen Breaker, Emberbrand Axe, Starwood Greataxe, Moonlit Reaper) take netherite ingots. Fishing rods take string or Tidescale. Two of the same tool also combine into one in an anvil. Your SkyRPG enchants stay on the tool.
Brannoc Ashforge, the Blacksmith. Hold the damaged tool and right-click Brannoc: he quotes a price for mending it completely, and a second right-click pays it. Sneak and right-click to open his shop as usual. The price is per missing durability point: 0.4 coins for Common, 0.6 Uncommon, 0.8 Rare, 1 Epic and 1.2 for Legendary tools (a completely worn-out Lumen Breaker costs about 4,800 coins).
Upgrading at the Artisan Bench gives you the next tool fully repaired, with the old one's name and enchantments.
The Unbreakable enchant means a tool never takes damage at all (see Enchanting).
Tools you already own start with full durability the next time they are in your inventory after this update.

The four accessory slots (amulet, cloak, belt, bracers), every accessory and where to get it.

Accessories are extra pieces of gear that sit outside your armour: an amulet, a cloak, a belt and a pair of bracers. They give stats like any other gear, they are kept when you die, and everyone nearby can see them on your character. There are 19 accessories, and you can wear one in each of the four slots at once.

A strip of four slots sits to the left of your armour in the inventory screen (press E), and on the creative inventory's Survival Inventory tab. It hides while the recipe book is open, because the book uses the same space.

Or shift-click it in your inventory, or drop it onto its slot. The slot lights up gold while you carry something that fits.
Each accessory only fits its own slot.
Accessories are stored with you, not in your inventory, so you keep them on death and /clear does not touch them.

A worn accessory adds its stats under the Accessories source on your Stats page (see Stats). Holding one in your hand gives nothing. Some accessories also have an effect, such as life steal or a dodge chance.

The seven shields from the Oak Buckler to the Astral Aegis: how much they block, their effects, the recipes and how to use them.

Shields are the first way to block damage in SkyRPG instead of just out-healing it. There are seven, one for each stage of the game, and each is bigger and more ornate than the last. They are crafted at the Artisan Bench, each one from the shield before it, and from the third on they come with an effect of their own.

Hold right-click with a shield in your off hand (or your main hand) to raise it. You block damage that comes from the front, within a quarter turn either side of where you are looking. A short moment passes after raising it before it works.
Each shield blocks a share of the damage: 50% for the Oak Buckler, up to 90% for the Astral Aegis. Your Defense works on what is left, so the two stack.
Fire, starving, magic and a few other kinds of damage get past any shield.
Axes knock a shield out of your hands for a few seconds, like in vanilla.
A shield is gear: its Defense and Health count while it is in your off hand (or your main hand), even when you are not blocking. Its effect works whenever it is held, and only blocking triggers it.
Shields never break. (Only gathering tools wear down: see Tools.)

A blocked melee hit shoves the attacker away from you, which gives you room to swing or run. The Skyiron Bulwark's shove is a good one, about a block and a half.

Every block now shows: a flash, a ring and sparks at the face of the shield (white for plain shields, embers for the Emberforged Aegis, ice for the Frostward Barrier, lightning for the Thunderguard, violet stars for the Astral Aegis), a crunching sound, and a short shake of your screen that grows with how hard the hit was. A Skyiron Bulwark bash adds a shove ring where the attacker was hit.

The Emberforged Aegis sets the attacker on fire when you block their hit, and the Frostward Barrier slows them heavily and frosts them for three seconds. Both only trigger on melee attackers that you actually block: hits from behind, and arrows, do not.

Every hit you block (melee or an arrow) stores a charge, up to five. A message on the action bar counts them, and each charge rings a higher chime (a bright note when you are full). Sneak and right-click to release them as a shockwave around you, a ring of lightning racing out of you and a bolt on every mob, one after another, with a screen shake: every hostile mob within 3 blocks plus 1 per charge takes lightning and 40 damage per charge, before your Strength and a crit roll. With five charges that is 200 damage to everything within 8 blocks, and the charges are gone. You cannot raise the shield while you are releasing.
Stand in a crowd with the Thunderguard up, take hits until the action bar says 5/5, then sneak and right-click. It is the best crowd-clearing move in the game before the Starfall Blade.

An arrow, a fireball or a trident that hits the raised Astral Aegis from the front is sent back at whoever shot it, a little faster. A reflected arrow becomes yours: it deals SkyRPG damage and counts for your kills. Projectiles from behind still hit you.

Every shield is a small 3D model: you see its thickness and raised rims in your hand, in the inventory and when you block. The Emberforged Aegis' cracks and the Thunderguard's veins glow in the dark, the Astral Aegis' stars twinkle, and the stronger ones shed particles (embers, snowflakes, sparks, motes of light).

The three backpack slots, the five pack sizes and how to upgrade them.

Backpacks give you more room to carry things. You carry up to three at once, each in its own slot, and you open them on the move without putting anything down. Mining and farming fill your bag fast, so a backpack is one of the first upgrades worth getting.

Three backpack slots sit in a strip to the right of the inventory in the E screen (and on the creative inventory's Survival Inventory tab). Like the accessory strip, it hides while the recipe book is open.

Backpacks cannot go inside backpacks.
A pack's contents are stored on the pack item, so it keeps them wherever it goes. Backpacks you carry are stored with you, so you keep them on death. The tooltip shows how full a pack is.

The seven SkyRPG bows, the first ranged weapons: how arrows deal damage, each bow's effect, recipes and enchants.

SkyRPG bows are real ranged weapons. They draw and shoot like vanilla bows and use ordinary arrows as ammo, but the arrows deal SkyRPG damage: the bow's Damage stat plus your Strength, Crit Chance and Crit Damage, the same way a sword does. There are seven, from the Hunter's Bow to the Starfall Bow. Each is crafted at the Artisan Bench from the bow before it, with logs from Foraging and the usual combat materials.

Damage per arrow is the bow's Damage stat times how far you drew it. A full draw (one second) is full damage; a half draw is about half. A shot weaker than a tenth of a draw does not fire.
Then your Strength adds 1% per point and a Crit Chance roll can multiply the hit by 1 + Crit Damage / 100, exactly like melee. The Strength and crit stats on your armour, talents and on the bow itself all count. See Stats.
The hit is a normal hit: damage numbers show above the target (crits in gold), a kill gives you the Combat XP, Valor Marks and loot, and it counts for slayer quests and bosses.
A bow's own stats (Strength, crits) only count while you hold it. Hitting something with the bow itself does almost nothing.
Bow enchants such as Deadeye (+damage), Splitshot, Longshot, Quiversong and Starshot work on all SkyRPG bows (see Enchanting).
Arrows are not used up by the extra arrows of the Starfall Bow, and its stars cannot be picked up again.

Each bow has its own arrow trail while the arrow flies: sparks for the Hunter's Bow, green motes for the Recurve, a thin smoke line for the Longbow, flames for the Ember Bow, snowflakes for the Frostbite Bow, electric sparks for the Stormcaller and stardust for the Starfall Bow.

Full draw: the moment a bow reaches full draw there is a glint at the arrow and a soft chime, so you know when to let go. A full-draw shot kicks the screen a little.
Hits: every arrow lands with a flash, a ring and sparks; the Ember Bow's is a fireball with embers and smoke, the Frostbite Bow's shatters ice, the Starfall Bow's bursts into stars and the Longbow's is a clean white streak.

Pierce: the Longbow's arrow flies through its first target and hits the next one, each for full damage.
Ember burst: a fire arrow sets what it hits alight, and bursts, hurting every hostile mob within 2.5 blocks for 60% of the hit. The burst never destroys blocks or starts fires on the ground.
Frost: the Frostbite Bow's hit slows the target to a crawl and frosts it for 3 seconds, which also makes it easy to hit again.
Lightning: the Stormcaller Bow counts your full-draw shots. The third one, then the sixth, and so on, calls a bolt of lightning on the target for 80% of the hit on top of it. Half-drawn shots do not count and do not reset the count.
Star arrows: the Starfall Bow's three arrows fan out a few degrees. Each deals 55% of the bow's Damage (a full hit with all three is 165%), and they bend towards enemies in front of them, so close shots on a single target often land all three.
The Ember Bow's burst makes it the bow for groups, the Longbow for lines of mobs in corridors, the Frostbite Bow for fast or dangerous melee mobs and bosses you want to keep at range.

Bow enchants (Deadeye, Longshot, Quiversong, Splitshot, Starshot, Cinder Arrows) can all be put on SkyRPG bows. Strength and crit stats from armour, accessories and talents apply to arrows too, so a melee build is a good ranged build as well.

Wands are the weapons of a mage build. A wand gives you Intelligence (more mana) while you hold it, has spell slots for spell scrolls, and turns the mouse into a spellcasting tool: left click casts the selected spell, hold right click opens the spell wheel. Each upgrade keeps the old wand's enchants and the scrolls inside it. The Skyiron Rod is the fork in the road: both epic staves and the Tempest Scepter are made from it; the Starweaver Staff then comes from the Tempest Scepter. Intelligence counts only while you hold the wand (like any held item), so your mana is 100 + Intelligence from the wand + your other gear. See Stats.
With a wand in your main hand the mouse is for spells:
Left click | Casts the selected spell. You do not swing and cannot break blocks.
Hold left click | Charges a chargeable spell (Fireball, Meteor) for up to 1.5 seconds. A ring fills around your crosshair and a chime rises; let go to cast. A full charge pings.
Hold right click | After a quarter of a second the spell wheel opens. Move the mouse towards a spell and release to select it.
Sneak + right click | Opens the wand's spell slots, where you put scrolls in and take them out.
Sneak + scroll wheel | Selects the next or previous spell.

Right click still does what it does on things that have a use of their own: chests, doors, levers, animals and NPCs. The wheel opens when you aim at the air, a plain block or an enemy. A shield in your off hand still raises. Two keys can be changed under Controls > SkyRPG: Spell wheel (hold), right click by default, and Spell wheel (toggle), G by default, which opens a wheel that stays open until you click a spell. See Controls and keys.

Your wand's spells sit round a circle in the middle of the screen, each with its icon, name, mana cost and, while recharging, the time left. The one under the mouse lights up in its element's colour and the middle says what it does. It pops open and shrinks away with a chime. A spell you cannot afford shows its cost in red.

While you hold a wand, a box on the HUD (bottom right; move it in the HUD editor) shows the selected spell: the icon, with the cooldown sweeping down over it, its name, its mana cost, a charge bar for chargeable spells and a pip for each slot. Without enough mana the cost flashes red and says so; casting a recharging spell tells you how long is left.

Sneak and right click with the wand open its slots: a row where the wand's slots sit in the middle and the rest are locked. Drop a spell scroll into a slot to install it (each spell only once per wand), shift-click to move it in, and take it out again to get the scroll back. The wand cannot be moved while its slots are open.

A mage build is a wand, Intelligence and mana: Intelligence makes every spell hit harder (each point adds 1% damage) and gives more mana for more casts. Mana returns at 2% of your maximum per second, so a bigger pool also refills faster. Spells do not use Strength or crits. They do count for combat XP, loot, kills and slayers like any hit of yours, and they never hurt your party members. See Spells for the twelve spells and how to get the scrolls.

Put a cheap fast spell (Firebolt or Frost Shard) in the first slot for everyday fights, and keep a Blink or a Mana Shield ready on the wheel for when things go wrong. The Astral Aegis in your off hand adds 25 Intelligence.

Every stat in SkyRPG, what it does, where it comes from and the formulas for damage, crits, defence and mana.

Stats are the numbers that make your character stronger. Gear, skill levels, pets, talents and slayer levels all add to them, and the game adds them up twice a second. This page lists every stat, what it does in the game, and the maths behind combat. Open the Stats page in the K menu to see your own totals; hover a stat to see how much each source adds.

Every player starts with a base value for each stat (the table below). Sources add to it.
Stats come from your armour, weapon, accessories and set bonuses, from your skill levels, from pets, from talents, and from slayer levels. See Skills overview, Armour sets, Accessories and Pets.
Most stats are plain numbers. Crit Chance and Sea Creature Chance are percentages.
Health and damage use SkyRPG's own scale: 5 SkyRPG health is 1 vanilla health point. 100 Health is 20 vanilla points, which is 10 hearts. Damage numbers, mob nameplates and boss bars all use the same scale.
More Health doesn't make you hungrier. Healing back to full costs the same hunger as it does in vanilla with 10 hearts, however much Health you have.
Health | 100 | Your maximum health. 100 Health is 10 hearts.
Defense | 0 | Cuts the damage you take. 100 Defense halves it.
Strength | 0 | Each point adds 1% to your melee damage.
Crit Chance | 30% | The chance that a melee hit is a critical hit.
Crit Damage | 50% | The extra damage a critical hit does.
Speed | 100 | How fast you walk. 100 is normal.
Intelligence | 0 | Each point adds 1 to your maximum mana and 1% to your spell damage. Abilities and spells cost mana.
Damage | none | Only weapons have it. It is the weapon's base damage.
Only your own melee hits use Strength and crits. Arrows, thrown things and item abilities do not.

Start with the weapon's Damage stat. A weapon with 120 Damage deals 120 on a fully charged swing (internally, 5 Damage is 1 vanilla damage point). If you swing before your weapon has recharged, the hit is weaker, as in vanilla.
Multiply by 1 + Strength / 100. Strength 100 doubles the hit.
Roll for a crit. If a random number from 0 to 100 is below your Crit Chance, multiply by 1 + Crit Damage / 100. Crits show a gold, bold number between two sparkles and play a crit sound.
Other multipliers apply on top, multiplied together: damage bonuses against certain mobs (slayer weapons and the Cryptbreaker), and the damage reductions bosses have (wards, tougher-than-vanilla health). See Slayers and Dungeons overview.
Worked example: a 120 Damage weapon, 100 Strength, 30% Crit Chance and 50% Crit Damage.
Average over many hits | 240 x (1 + 0.30 x 0.50) = 276
Crit Chance above 100% is wasted: you already crit every time. Crit Damage is then worth more than more Crit Chance.

Crit Chance and Crit Damage multiply each other, so the lower one is worth more per point. A point of Crit Chance adds 1% of your Crit Damage to your average hit, and a point of Crit Damage adds 1% of your Crit Chance. With the starting 30% and 50%, a point of Crit Chance is the better buy.
Every time something hurts you, the damage is multiplied by 100 / (100 + Defense).

So "effective health" is Health x (1 + Defense / 100). Defense applies to mobs, bosses, traps, fire and falling. It does not apply to damage that ignores invulnerability, such as the void. Armour pieces give Defense directly (they have no vanilla armour points). Slayer armour wards and similar reductions apply before Defense.
Speed 100 is normal walking. Walking speed is multiplied by Speed / 100, so 150 Speed walks 50% faster.

You have 100 + Intelligence maximum mana. Mana regenerates by 2% of your maximum every second, so an empty bar takes about 50 seconds to refill whatever its size. Item abilities and spells spend mana when you use them. A mage's wand gives Intelligence while held, and each point also adds 1% to the damage of your spells (Strength and crits do not apply to spells). If your maximum drops (you take off a piece of gear), your current mana is cut to fit.
Mining Speed | 0 | How fast you break blocks. 100 makes it twice as fast.
Mining Fortune | 0 | Extra drops from ores, stone, sand and everything else that gives Mining XP.
Farming Fortune | 0 | Extra drops from crops.
Foraging Fortune | 0 | Extra drops from logs.
Fishing Speed | 0 | Fish bite sooner. Every 25 is one more level of Lure, up to four.
Sea Creature Chance | 5% | The chance a catch is a sea creature instead of a fish.
Fishing Fortune | 0 | More Tidescales from catches. Every 100 is one more.

When you break a block that counts (ores, grown crops, logs), it drops its normal drops again once for every full 100 Fortune, plus a chance for one more from the remainder. With 250 Fortune you get 2 extra copies and a 50% chance of a third. Crops only count when fully grown, and ores do not give extra drops if you mine them with Silk Touch. See Mining, Farming and Foraging.
Farming Insight | Each point is 1% more Farming XP.
Mining Insight | Each point is 1% more Mining XP.
Foraging Insight | Each point is 1% more Foraging XP.
Combat Insight | Each point is 1% more Combat XP.
Fishing Insight | Each point is 1% more Fishing XP.
Enchanting Insight | Each point is 1% more Enchanting XP.
Delving Insight | Each point is 1% more Delving XP.
Magic Find | Better odds for rare drops from mobs and bosses.
Insight multiplies the XP you earn playing by 1 + Insight / 100. Every skill has one; where it comes from is on Skills overview.

Magic Find multiplies the chance of rare drops by 1 + Magic Find / 100. 50 Magic Find makes a 1 in 400 drop 1.5 times as likely. It helps with Valor Marks, Dread Fang, Nightmare Core, slayer rare drops and Golden Pet Eggs, and with enchant tome drops. It does not change the world bosses' own rare drop chance. See Combat basics.
Skills give a fixed amount per level (50 levels each). Delving has talents too.
Slayer levels add a small stat per level too: Grave Tyrant +3 Health, Broodmother +0.5% Crit Chance, Bone Marshal +1 Strength, Void Stalker +2 Intelligence. See Slayers.
Weapon Damage is not a player stat. Only the weapon you hold carries it, and nothing can add to it.

Every hostile mob in the survival world has a level. The higher the level, the more health it has, the harder it hits and the more it pays when it dies. This page explains how levels are set, what you see in a fight, and what a kill rewards you with. Kestrel Vane, the weaponsmith in Skyhaven, is the Combat Master and buys most of what drops.
A hostile mob gets its level when it spawns. Mobs in the hub never get one.
Overworld surface | 1 at world spawn, +1 for every 120 blocks away, up to level 30
The Nether | 20, +1 for every 180 blocks from the world spawn
The End | 40, +1 for every 480 blocks from the world spawn
The result is capped at 50 first. Then extra levels are added on top, past the cap:

Danger regions: +12 to +20 depending on the region. See Danger regions.
Deep layers: +4 (Glimmer Caverns), +7 (Fungal Depths), +10 (Dwarven Halls layer) and +14 (Magma Rifts). See The Deep.
Blood Moon: +10 everywhere in the overworld. See Blood Moon.
Dungeons: each dungeon sets its own levels. See Dungeons overview.
Each level above 1 adds 8% health and 5% damage (multiplied, not stacked on the Elite bonus).
Mobs you spawn with a spawn egg or a command are levelled too, so test mobs behave like real ones.

When you can see a levelled mob and it is within 20 blocks, it shows a plate like [Lv 12] Zombie 85/100. The level is green below 10, yellow below 20, gold below 30, red below 40 and dark red from 40. The health is on the same scale as your own health bar (5 SkyRPG health is 1 vanilla point) and turns yellow below half and red below a quarter. Bosses stronger than vanilla health allows show their real health, not the capped number. You can switch plates off in Settings under HUD ("Mob nameplates").

Each hit you land pops a number up in front of the mob for under a second. Normal hits are grey. Critical hits are bold gold between two white sparkles. The number is the damage as the stats work it out: see Stats.

Fighting puts you in combat for 10 seconds. While you are, a red In combat box with the seconds left shows at the top of the screen, and you cannot teleport away: /hub, /survival and waystone trips are refused with the time left. See The Survival World and Waystones and Travel.

deal damage to a hostile mob or another player, or take damage from one
are hit by a projectile or ability, or hit with one yourself (an arrow counts for whoever fired it)

Each new hit restarts the 10 seconds. These do not tag you: fall damage, fire, lava, drowning, starving, the void and other damage that has no attacker, or hitting a cow or other passive animal. Dying clears the tag. Creative and spectator players are never tagged.
The numbers (10 seconds of tag, 5 second warm-up, how far you may drift) are data in data/skyrpg_core/skyrpg/combat/rules.json.
Some naturally spawned hostile mobs are Elites. They never appear in the hub.
Underground (below y 40 with no open sky) | 8%

A Blood Moon makes Elites three times as likely everywhere. An Elite is three levels higher than it would have been, has 4 times the health, +50% damage, is 10% faster and 15% bigger, shows a gold Elite nameplate and glitters. Elites in dungeons are placed on purpose and also carry the dungeon's vault key: see Dungeons overview.

50 to 200 coins and 40 Combat XP
an Elite Trophy (Kestrel buys them for 250 coins)
3 extra Valor Marks, on top of the normal level rewards
a 1 in 50 chance of a Lucky Clover or a Prism Fragment
The Elite Hunt contract asks for 3 to 6 Elites and pays 1,200 coins, 800 Combat XP and 2 Elite Trophies. See Contracts.
Killing a levelled mob (with a melee hit, or an arrow you fired) gives:

Combat XP. The base XP for that kind of mob (a zombie or skeleton is 6, an enderman 12, a wither skeleton 15) plus 1.5 per mob level. Combat Insight raises it. See Skills overview.
Valor Marks. A chance of 25% + 1% per level (capped at 100%) to drop 1 + 1 per 15 levels Valor Marks.
A Dread Fang or a Nightmare Core, rarely (see below).
The mob's normal drops.

Nine Valor Marks craft into one Valor Seal (a 3 by 3 grid), and a seal can be split back into nine. Kestrel takes marks as payment for the Fangguard armour and a Pup Egg. Seals go into slayer gear and swords. See Weapons and Armour sets.

At most one of the two drops per kill, and a core is rolled first. Magic Find multiplies both chances by 1 + Magic Find / 100. A message tells you when one drops. Kestrel buys fangs for 1,200 coins and cores for 15,000.

Mobs from a spawner (including the spawners you buy from Morwen) and the helpers some mobs call in (Gravecaller zombies, Bog Hag slimes) are farmed. They drop their normal loot and give only a quarter of the level XP. They give no Valor Marks, no fangs or cores, never become Elites and do not count for slayer quests. See Slayers.
The Training Dummy is a mannequin you place to test your gear.

Kestrel Vane sells it for 500 coins. Place it by right-clicking a block.
Hit it and the action bar shows your damage per second over the last 5 seconds and your last hit.
It never dies, and only players can hurt it.
Each hit gives 0.5 Combat XP, up to 150 Combat XP per hour, so it cannot be left running.
Sneak and hit it with an empty hand to pick it up again.
Swap a piece of gear, hit the dummy for ten seconds, and compare the DPS. It is the quickest way to find out whether a reforge or an enchant is worth it.

Every custom SkyRPG mob: where it spawns, how tough it is, its tricks and what it drops.

SkyRPG adds its own monsters on top of vanilla's. Each one is a new kind of mob built on a vanilla body, with its own look, attacks and drops. They get levels, nameplates and damage numbers like any other hostile mob, they can be Elites, and several of them count for slayer quests. This page is the field guide. For the full item list of any drop, see the mob list.
Health in this page is the base health on the SkyRPG scale (5 health is 1 vanilla point), before the level bonus of +8% per level above 1. See Combat basics.
These eight spawn naturally, mostly in the dark. Spawn weight is compared with vanilla's zombie at 95.
Glimmer Crawler | caves below y 0 | 40 | 100 | Broodmother
Bog Hag | swamps, mangrove swamps | 25 | 200 | none
Frost Revenant | snowy biomes | 40 | 150 | Bone Marshal
Ember Imp | badlands (30), the Nether (10), Ember Forest (60) | see left | 70 | none
Grove Sentinel | forests except dark forests and pale gardens | 30 | 220 | none
Tide Lurker | rivers and beaches | 35 | 150 | Grave Tyrant
Hollow Wisp | plains, sunflower plains, meadows | 15 | 80 | Void Stalker
Gravecaller | dark forests and pale gardens | 35 | 170 | Grave Tyrant

They follow the usual monster rule: on the ground, in the dark, so surface ones come out at night. Crawlers need to be below y 0. Danger regions, deep layers and Blood Moons add levels on top. See Danger regions.
A quick spider (speed 0.4, a quarter bigger than normal) with glowing crystals on its back. It lives in the caves below y 0 and comes in groups of 1 to 3.
Drops: 0 to 2 string, 1 to 3 Glimmer Shards, and a 1% chance of a Prism Fragment when a player kills it.
A swamp witch. While she fights you she calls bog slimes to her side: two every 15 seconds, four at most. The slimes are farmed, so they give nothing.
Drops: a Hag's Charm, 0 to 2 glass bottles, and a 10% chance of a Duskwillow sapling.
A stray of the snowy lands. Each arrow that hits you adds 6 seconds of freezing, the same slow as powder snow.
Drops: 0 to 2 bones, 0 to 2 arrows and 1 to 2 Rime Shards.
A small, quick blaze (65% size, speed 0.32) that throws fireballs. It is fire immune. Imps also fill the Ember Forest in the Nether and the Magma Tyrant calls them as helpers (see The Nether).
Drops: an Ember Core, 0 to 1 blaze powder and an 8% chance of an Emberwood sapling.

A slow, tough guardian of the forests, built on a zombie body with 6 armour and 60% knockback resistance. It is made of wood: it does not burn in daylight, has no baby form and calls no reinforcements. Its hits give Slowness IV for 2 seconds, which roots you in place. Base damage 25.
Drops: 1 to 3 sticks, 1 to 2 Heartwood Splinters and a 2.5% chance of a Golden Acorn.
Do not stand and trade blows with a Grove Sentinel. Hit it, step back, and let the root wear off before you step in again. It walks slowly, so a bow keeps you out of reach.

A drowned that haunts rivers and beaches at night. Every 6 seconds, if you are 4 to 12 blocks away and it can see you, it throws a tide hook and hauls you towards it (and towards the water). Base damage 20. Tide Lurkers also guard the Drowned Temple.
Drops: 0 to 2 rotten flesh, 1 to 2 Tidescales and a 3% chance of a nautilus shell.
A lone spirit that drifts through walls, unarmed. It is small and flies, so fight it in the open. Base damage 15.
Drops: a Wisp Essence and 0 to 2 glowstone dust.

A necromancer of the dark forests. Within 16 blocks of its target it raises two zombies every 12 seconds, four at most. The zombies are farmed, so killing them is for safety, not for rewards. Kill the Gravecaller first.
Drops: rotten flesh and bones (0 to 2 each) and a 50% chance of Tyrant's Ash.

See The Deep and The Nether for the places themselves.

A knee-high mushroom creature, speed 0.32, base damage 15. Sporelings keep to their group and the whole group joins in when one of them finds you or is hit (within 12 blocks). When one dies it bursts into a spore cloud (3 blocks wide, about 4 seconds) that gives Poison for 5 seconds. Sporelings and their kin are immune to the poison.
Drops: 0 to 1 brown mushroom and a 30% chance of Glowcap Spores.
Kill Sporelings with a bow or step back as soon as one dies. The cloud only reaches about 3 blocks.

A stone-and-brass automaton: 10 armour, 4 toughness, slow (speed 0.18), 75% knockback resistance, base damage 40. Arrows and other projectiles do half damage (with a spark and a clang). Its punch knocks you back and lifts you off your feet. The Forgeguard champion of the Dwarven Halls is a scaled-up Construct. See Dwarven Halls.
Drops: a copper nugget (3 in 5) or an iron nugget (2 in 5), 1 to 4 or 1 to 3, and a 20% chance of a Dwarven Cog. In the layer, kills also have their own 25% chance of a Dwarven Cog.

A big six-legged beetle with a magma-cracked shell: 8 armour, 2 toughness, 75% knockback resistance, base damage 30, fire immune. Its bite sets you alight for 4 seconds. Every 7.5 seconds, if you are 4 to 12 blocks away and in sight, it digs in for one second (the wing cases lift, flames at its feet), then dashes about 12 blocks in a straight line. A hit does 1.8 times its normal damage, a big knockback and sets you alight for 5 seconds. A wall or a hit ends the dash early.
Drops: 0 to 2 magma cream and a 25% chance of a Rift Ember.
When the beetle digs in, sidestep. The charge goes in a straight line, so stepping out of its path is enough.
A hunched giant skeleton: 550 health, 8 armour, 2 toughness, 80% knockback resistance, base damage 60, fire immune. It walks over soul sand without sinking.

Club swing: it raises its femur club and brings it down 11 ticks later, about every 1.6 seconds, with heavy knockback and a lift.
Bone quake: about every 10 seconds, with you within 5 blocks, it rears up for a second while a ring of soul fire marks the ground. Then it stomps: everyone within 4 blocks takes 75% of its attack damage, is thrown up a little and is slowed for 3 seconds.
Drops: 2 to 5 bones, a 35% chance of 1 to 2 bone blocks, a 50% chance of 1 to 3 soul soil, and a 12% chance (player kills) of a Hellforged Scrap.
Leave the ring of soul fire before the stomp lands. The quake is only dangerous if you are inside it.

Morwen Ashgrave's slayer quests, the four lines and their bosses, slayer levels, slayer gear and the spawner ladder.

Slayers are the combat endgame. Morwen Ashgrave, the Slayer Master, has a market stall in Skyhaven next to the Curio Dealer. She sells slayer quests: you pay a fee, hunt a kind of mob until a bar fills, and a boss rises to fight you. Beat it and you earn slayer XP, tokens and rare drops, which turn into the best combat gear before the dungeons. She also sells mob spawners. Talking to her opens a screen with two tabs, Slayer Quests and Spawners. The same quests appear on the Slayers page in the K menu.

Pick a line and a tier on Morwen's screen and pay the fee.
Kill that line's mobs anywhere in the survival world. Each kill fills the quest bar by 1 + mob level / 5, so higher level mobs fill it faster. Mobs from spawners do not count.
When the bar is full, the slayer boss rises next to you with a boss bar and a clock.
Kill it before time runs out. Friends can help.
If time runs out or you die, the quest fails and the fee is gone.

Your quest and its timer show on the HUD. The boss hunts the player who started the quest, and follows them: a boss more than 32 blocks away, or one that has not hit anything for 15 seconds, comes to them. If you log off, change dimension, go to the hub or enter spectator mode, the boss leaves, and it comes back with the time that was left.
Bosses with more than 5,120 health (vanilla's cap) are made tougher another way: they take proportionally less damage. Their nameplate and your damage numbers show the real values.
Grave Tyrant | zombies, husks, drowned, zombie villagers, Tide Lurkers and Gravecallers | Tyrant's Ash | Plague Heart | +3 Health
Broodmother | spiders, cave spiders and Glimmer Crawlers | Brood Silk | Venom Gland | +0.5% Crit Chance
Bone Marshal | skeletons, strays, bogged, wither skeletons and Frost Revenants | Marrow Shard | Marshal's Sigil | +1 Strength
Void Stalker | endermen, endermites and Hollow Wisps | Void Fragment | Null Core | +2 Intelligence
Zombified piglins do not count for the Grave Tyrant, so gold farms do not help. See Mobs for the custom mobs.
Each boss's size grows with the tier, and every tier is a new, more armoured form with its own model.

Combat XP is a twentieth of the boss's health. The rare drop and egg chances are raised by Magic Find. The usual rewards for killing a high-level mob (Valor Marks, fangs, cores) apply on top. Each kill also gives the slayer XP from the tier table, which is what levels the line.

The tier sets a multiplier on the boss's normal attack. Many signature moves (Grave Slam, Pounce, Void Bolt, the plague aura, rifts) instead hurt by a share of your maximum health, so they matter at any gear level. Defense still reduces the result.
Every line has its own level, 1 to 9, from the slayer XP you earn on it.
Each level gives its line's stat from the table above, permanently. Levels also unlock things:
2 | Tier II quests, and the slayer boots
4 | Tier III quests, and the slayer helmet
6 | Tier IV quests, and the line's legendary weapon

Every tier adds one attack and one defence on top of the tiers below, so a tier IV fight uses everything the line has. Every attack is announced in the action bar and marked on the ground before it lands.

I | Risen Tyrant: Grave Slam. Rotting Hide (projectiles do half) | Brood Mother: Web Shot. Chitin Plates (melee does 20% less) | Bone Sergeant: Volley. Bone Plating (no knockback) | Void Wanderer: Void Bolt, blinks behind you. Phase Step (dodges 1 hit in 5)

II | Plague Tyrant: Raise the Dead. Life Drain (heals 2% per hit, enrages below half) | Venom Matron: Pounce. Brood Shield (takes 70% less while 3 or more brood live) | Bone Captain: Arrow Rain, bigger volleys. Tactical Retreat | Void Seeker: Void Grasp (pulls you in, blinding hits). Null Shield

III | Dread Tyrant: Gravestones. Bone Armour (60% less damage for 3 seconds after each slam) | Silk Empress: Egg Sacs and Brood. Silk Cocoon (heals at half health) | Bone Commander: Piercing Shot. War Banner | Void Reaver: Void Beacon. Mirror Images

IV | Tyrant King: Plague Aura and Tomb Prison. Undying (rises once) | Brood Queen Arachnia: Silk Prison and Venom Bite. Venom Blood | Bone Marshal Supreme: Legion. Bone Shield | Void Sovereign: Rifts and Void Collapse. Void Siphon

Grave Slam every 12 seconds: a roar, a leap and a shockwave on a marked circle. It takes 13% of your maximum health at tier I and 22% at tier IV.
Enrage below half health from tier II: faster and harder hitting.
Raise the Dead every 15 seconds from tier II: 2 zombies (3 at tier IV).
Gravestones every 15 seconds from tier III: tombstones fall on marked circles. Break them before they burst.
Plague Aura (tier IV): every second, everyone near it loses 4% of their maximum health. Tomb Prison seals you in stone. Undying: the first time it dies it gets back up with 35% of its health.

The Tyrant King's aura takes a share of your health every second, so a long fight hurts. Bring a weapon with strong damage against the line (Gravebane) or the Gravewarden set, and kill the zombies it raises quickly.

Web Shot every 8 seconds slows you to a crawl.
Pounce every 9 seconds from tier II, from 4 to 18 blocks away. It hits for 12% to 16% of your maximum health and slows you.
Egg Sacs at two thirds and one third health from tier III: 3 or 4 sacs that hatch two spiderlings each after 6 seconds unless you hit them twice. She also hatches cave spiders (3, or 4 at tier IV) every 15 seconds.
Silk Cocoon (tier III and up): below half health she cocoons and heals 3% of her health a second, taking almost no damage. Cut her out with 6 hits (8 at tier IV).
Silk Prison (tier IV) webs you in place, then she pounces. Venom Blood: hitting her from within 5 blocks poisons you.
Kill the brood first. While three or more spiders live, the Venom Matron takes 70% less damage.

Volley every 10 seconds: 3 arrows, 5 from tier II.
Arrow Rain every 14 seconds from tier II on a marked circle under you.
Tactical Retreat from tier II: it leaps away when you get too close.
Piercing Shot from tier III: it draws its greatbow first. Break line of sight.
War Banner below half health from tier III: it takes half damage and heals 1% a second until you tear the banner down (3 hits, 5 at tier IV).
Legion and Bone Shield (tier IV): it calls archers and a bone knight, and every 20 seconds raises a shield that stops most damage for 4 seconds.

Void Bolt every 8 seconds: 8% (tier I) to 14% (tier IV) of your maximum health, plus Darkness. It also blinks behind you every 10 seconds.
Null Shield from tier II, at two thirds and one third health: you must land 5 hits (8 at tier III, 12 at tier IV) to break it.
Void Beacon every 20 seconds from tier III: a beacon that detonates for half your health unless you break it in 6 seconds.
Mirror Images (tier III) split off Void Echoes, and it takes half damage while they live.
Rifts (tier IV): rifts burst under you for a quarter of your maximum health. At a quarter of its health it triggers Void Collapse, and Void Siphon heals it whenever rifts or the collapse hurt someone.
Gear is made at the Artisan Bench, on its Slayer tab, from the line's token, Valor Seals and a filler. See Crafting.
Each costs 32 tokens, 4 Valor Seals and a filler.

Set bonus (all four pieces): you take 30% less damage from that line's mobs and its boss, deal 10% more to them, and earn 25% more slayer XP from that line's bosses. The reduction applies before Defense. The set also gives stats:
The Voidwalker set also has a slow orbit of void shards around you. See Armour sets and Weapons.
Morwen sells spawners in a fixed order, the spawner ladder. The first is open to everyone. Each next one unlocks once you have killed 5,000 of the mob before it (your lifetime kills count).

Steps unlock in order, so 5,000 zombie kills from normal play do not skip you past the chickens. A bought spawner places like a block. Breaking one you placed gives it back, with no XP. Spawners found in dungeons stay vanilla and drop nothing.
Mobs from spawners are farmed: normal loot, a quarter of the level XP, and no Valor Marks, rare drops or Elites. They do not count for slayer quests. A spawner is for materials, not for levelling.

The Hollow King and the Mother of Thorns, the server-wide bosses that rise in the survival world, and the region bosses.

World bosses are events. Every couple of hours a huge boss rises in the survival world near a random player, the whole server is told where, and everyone who hurts it is paid by how much damage they did. There are two of them, the Hollow King and the Mother of Thorns. They are the best source of Valor Seals outside the slayer quests, with a real chance at a Nightmare Core or Dread Fang.

Every 2 to 3 hours (random), if two or more players are online, the game picks a world boss at random. If an op uses /worldboss start, it can be sooner.
It picks a random player in the overworld and chooses a spot 14 to 26 blocks from them, on dry land.
A chat message with a warning sound goes to everyone: the boss stirs near that player, with coordinates, and rises one minute later. Soul flames show where.
When it rises, lightning strikes and a second message gives the coordinates again.
Only one world boss is up at a time.
If nobody kills it in 15 minutes, it sinks back into the earth and nobody is paid.
A boss bar shows its health to everyone within 64 blocks.
The warning gives you a minute. Grab your best weapon and armour, a stack of food and arrows, and a friend. The more people hit it, the faster it falls, and everyone who deals damage is paid.
Body | giant wither skeleton | giant spider
Damage | 2.5 times the body's normal attack | 2.5 times the body's normal attack
Both have full knockback resistance, so you cannot push them around.

Ground slam, every 8 seconds. Everyone within 6 blocks takes damage (10 vanilla damage points, which is 50 Health, before your Defense) and is thrown back. Keep your distance, or stay behind it when you see the particles.
Minions at two thirds health. The boss calls its helpers in a ring around it and warns you. They are level 25 and level 20 mobs, so kill them quickly or fight away from them.
Minions again at one third health, and the boss enrages. At one third health the boss gets 30% faster.
Minions disappear when the boss dies or leaves. Creative and spectator players are not hit by the slam.

Ranged weapons are the safest way to damage a world boss. Stay outside the 6 block slam ring, shoot, and move away when it calls minions. Armour with plenty of Defense and Health makes a slam survivable, and a Training Dummy tells you how much damage your build really does. See Stats.
Everyone who damaged the boss is paid when it falls, whether or not they landed the last hit. The top damager gets half again (x1.5) of the coins, seals, Combat XP and rare drop chance.
Rare drop | Nightmare Core, 8% | Dread Fang, 40%
Bonus drop | Golden Pet Egg, 6% | Golden Pet Egg, 6%

The top damager's rare drop chance is 12% (Hollow King) or 60% (Mother of Thorns). The rare and bonus drops are rolled separately for each player, and Magic Find does not change these chances. A chat message shows what you earned and where you ranked.
A Nightmare Core sells for 15,000 coins and a Dread Fang for 1,200. A Golden Pet Egg is one of the rarest drops in the game. See Pets.

Danger regions have bosses of their own. They do not rise on a timer. You wake one by using a Heart Sigil at the region's shrine, or during a Blood Moon, when each heart wakes its boss if someone comes near. They are fought in the same way as a dungeon boss, with their own moves.
The Haunted Moors | The Lantern Wraith | 42 | 18,000
The Ashen Wastes | The Ash Colossus | 50 | 30,000
The Shattered Highlands | The Storm Griffin | 55 | 34,000
See Danger regions, Region hearts and Blood Moon.

The twelve spells of the wands: what each does, mana and cooldown, charging, and where to get every scroll.

Spells are what wands cast. Each spell is a scroll you install in a wand's slot; the wand's selected spell is the one left click casts. There are twelve in five elements: Fire, Frost, Lightning, Arcane and Nature. A spell costs mana and has a cooldown (the time before you can cast that spell again, shown as a sweep on the HUD box and on the spell wheel). Two spells can be charged: hold left click and let go.

Spell damage is the spell's base damage times (1 + Intelligence / 100), so Intelligence from your wand and gear makes every spell stronger. Your wand may add more: the Emberheart Staff adds 25% to fire spells and the Frostspire Staff 25% to frost spells.
A spell hit is a normal hit as far as everything else goes: damage numbers appear over the target, kills give you Combat XP, Valor Marks and loot, and they count for slayer quests and bosses. Strength and crits do not apply; Intelligence does the same job.
Spells never hurt you, your party members, your pets, NPCs or villagers. Other players are only hit where player fighting is allowed. Area spells and chains go for hostile mobs; a bolt hits whatever it touches.
Fireballs and meteors break no blocks and start no fires. Burning is the spell's own damage over time and counts as your damage too, but water puts it out.
Mana is 100 + your Intelligence and refills 2% of the maximum a second. See Stats.
Firebolt | Fire | Common | 8 | 0.5 s | A fast bolt for 35 damage that burns for 3 seconds (8 a second).

Fireball | Fire | Uncommon | 24 | 3 s | Chargeable. Explodes on impact: 70 damage in a 3 block radius (less towards the edge) and burns for 4 seconds. Fully charged, the blast is 5.5 blocks wide and hits twice as hard.

Meteor | Fire | Legendary | 60 | 12 s | Chargeable. A ring marks where you aim, and a meteor crashes there 1.3 seconds later for 170 damage in 5 blocks and 5 seconds of burning. Charged: 8 blocks and double damage.
Frost Shard | Frost | Common | 7 | 0.6 s | A fast shard that pierces up to 3 enemies, 32 damage each, and slows them (Slowness III for 2.5 seconds).
Blizzard | Frost | Rare | 50 | 14 s | A snowstorm where you aim, 5 blocks wide, for 6 seconds: 24 damage twice a second and a slow on everything inside.

Chain Lightning | Lightning | Rare | 22 | 2.5 s | A bolt for 52 damage that leaps between up to 4 enemies within 7 blocks of each other (5 with the Tempest Scepter). With nothing to hit it fizzles and costs nothing.
Thunderclap | Lightning | Epic | 38 | 8 s | Thunder rolls out from you: everything within 6 blocks takes 62 damage, is thrown back and stunned for 1.4 seconds.
Arcane Missiles | Arcane | Uncommon | 26 | 4 s | Three homing missiles fan out and bend towards your enemies, 30 damage each.
Blink | Arcane | Uncommon | 16 | 6 s | Teleports you up to 8 blocks the way you look, as far as there is room and a safe floor. Never into a wall or lava. With no room it costs nothing.
Mana Shield | Arcane | Rare | 30 | 20 s | For 8 seconds damage you take is paid from your mana instead, half a mana per point. When the mana runs out the shield breaks and the hit lands.
Healing Pulse | Nature | Common | 30 | 6 s | A wave of green light that heals you and party members within 8 blocks for 60 health.
Entangle | Nature | Uncommon | 25 | 9 s | Vines root every enemy in a 4 block circle where you aim for 4 seconds and hurt them for 14 a second.
Firebolt Scroll | Common |  | 150 coins | Sold by Seraphine's Scrolls for 500 coins
Frost Shard Scroll | Common |  | 150 coins | Sold by Seraphine's Scrolls for 500 coins
Healing Pulse Scroll | Common |  | 200 coins | Sold by Seraphine's Scrolls for 700 coins
Damage is shown in SkyRPG damage, the same unit as weapon damage and the numbers over mobs. The figures in the table are before Intelligence and wand bonuses: with 100 Intelligence, double.

Fireball and Meteor can be charged. Hold left click with the spell selected: a ring fills around your crosshair (about 1.5 seconds) with a rising chime, then pings when it is full. Let go to cast. A quick tap casts the small version. Mana is checked when you start and spent when the spell goes off. Switching the held item cancels a charge, and so does anything that leaves you unable to cast when you let go (no mana, or the spell still recharging).
Common (Firebolt, Frost Shard, Healing Pulse) | Seraphine Vael at the Arcane Library sells them: 500, 500 and 700 coins. Sneak and talk to her. See NPCs.
Uncommon (Fireball, Blink, Arcane Missiles, Entangle) | The Artisan Bench, Enchanting 8 to 10: paper, Runic Dust and materials of the element.
Rare (Chain Lightning, Blizzard, Mana Shield) | The Artisan Bench, Enchanting 20 to 22, and they drop from bosses.

Epic (Thunderclap) and Legendary (Meteor) | Drop only, from the hardest bosses and dungeon rewards (the Ender Wyrm, the Star Warden, the Iron Thane and others), at a low chance. A Blood Moon also makes hostile mobs you kill drop a scroll now and then (not a Meteor).

Scrolls can be sold to the NPCs and traded. Installing one in a wand does not use it up: take it out again and you have it back. Scroll recipes: Fireball (paper, Ember Core, Blaze Powder), Blink (paper, Ender Pearl, Amethyst Shard), Arcane Missiles (paper, Amethyst, Wisp Essence), Entangle (paper, Vine, Dew Vial), Chain Lightning (paper, Stormfeather, Skyiron Ingot), Blizzard (paper, Rime Shard, Frost Essence) and Mana Shield (paper, Glimmer Crystal, Wisp Essence), all with Runic Dust.

Every spell flashes at the wand when it goes off and has its own trail, impact burst and sound.
Meteor, Thunderclap, a charged Fireball and the start of a Blizzard shake the screen for anyone close.
Lightning is drawn as jagged arcs between targets; a Thunderclap also calls lightning on a few of the enemies it stuns.
A Mana Shield circles you with blue light, flashes when it absorbs a hit and says how much it took.
