How SkyRPG dungeons work: finding them, mobs, traps, puzzles, keys, champions, bosses, per-player loot, resets and the Delving skill.

Dungeons are real structures in the world, generated from the seed like villages. You find one, walk in, fight through it, and it is still there tomorrow. There are eight, from the Forgotten Crypt at level 12 to the Astral Observatory at level 64. Each one has two or three floors, packs of mobs, traps, puzzles, a champion mini-boss and a final boss. Loot is per player, so friends never race each other for chests. Clearing dungeons is also how you level the Delving skill and get the gear that makes the next dungeon possible.
Forgotten Crypt | forests, plains, meadows | 12 | 12 to 19 | The Bone Knight | The Crypt Warden
Spider Hollow | dark forests, pale gardens | 22 | 19 to 26 | The Silk Matron | Queen Arachne
Drowned Temple | oceans, on the sea floor | 28 | 26 to 34 | The Abyssal Herald | The Tidemother
Dwarven Halls | under mountains, hills, forests | 34 | 32 to 41 | The Forgeguard | The Iron Thane
Infernal Citadel | the Nether | 48 | 44 to 52 | The Infernal Knight | The Magma Tyrant
Ruined Citadel | mountain peaks | 56 | 54 to 58 | The Knight-Captain | The Fallen Knight
Catacombs | deep underground, sealed | 62 | 59 to 62 | three Bone Wardens | The Bonelord
Astral Observatory | the outer End islands | 64 | 60 to 65 | The Astral Sentinel | The Star Warden
Nothing stops you entering early. The levels are a guide to how tough the mobs are. Compare them with the levels on your mobs' nameplates (see Combat basics) and with your Stats.
Each dungeon has a rarity. The spacing is the size, in chunks, of the grid cell that gets one attempt.
Astral Observatory | 26 | outer End islands only, 6 chunks from End cities
Drowned Temple | 32 | not in frozen oceans
Dwarven Halls | 40 | 8 chunks from Spider Hollows
Infernal Citadel | 44 | 8 chunks from vanilla fortresses and bastions
Spider Hollow | 18 | 10 chunks from Forgotten Crypts
Ruined Citadel | 56 | 10 chunks from Dwarven Halls
Catacombs | 64 | very rare, no surface part

Treasure maps. The Crypt Warden has a 40% chance of a Spider Hollow map, and Queen Arachne a 40% chance of a Drowned Temple map. Wayshrine chests can hold a Forgotten Crypt map (25%), and Abandoned Mine Camp chests a Dwarven Halls map (15%). Use them like vanilla explorer maps.
Waystones. Every dungeon entrance except the Catacombs has a waystone, so once you attune to it you can travel back. See Waystones and travel.
The questline. The Skyhaven Chronicle has a quest for most dungeons. Track the quest in your journal and a waypoint points at the nearest matching dungeon within 100 chunks (1,600 blocks). This is the way to find the Catacombs, which has no surface part. See Quests and journal and Waypoints.
Exploring. The deeper dungeons have no map. Look for them in the places listed in the table above.
Walking within 20 blocks of an entrance discovers it: a banner, a sound, a marker on the map and minimap, and an entry in your journal. Discovery also gives Delving XP.
A dungeon is a chain of rooms built from a seed, so no two are the same. Every dungeon has:

Floors. Most have two floors joined by a stairwell or descent. The Ruined Citadel has three, and the Catacombs is one huge labyrinth. Each floor is a spine of big halls with side rooms branching off them.
A champion arena at the end of the first floor, whose gate stays shut until the champion falls. (The Catacombs have three Bone Warden chambers instead.)
A boss arena at the end, about 31 by 15 by 31 blocks.
A vault behind a locked door, with the best chests.
Side rooms: libraries, barracks, shrines, treasuries, puzzle rooms, and small hidden caches.

Mobs wait in packs of 4 to 12, and many packs come in waves: the next wave spawns when the one before it is dead. A pack wakes when you come within about 10 blocks. Dungeon mobs never despawn. Packs are levelled by floor, and they pay the usual combat rewards: Combat XP, Valor Marks and the rest (see Combat basics).
Elites in packs are tougher and glow, and each has a 35% chance to drop the dungeon's vault key. When every mob from a room's packs is dead, the room is cleared. Some gates only open then.
Traps only work while a player is nearby.
Arrows | An arrow slit in a wall shoots the nearest player it can see.
Spikes | Hurt anyone standing on or close to them. They are marked with crit particles.
Flames | A fire burst that sets players on fire.
Trap damage is in vanilla damage points (1 point is 5 Health) before your Defense.
Arrow slits are iron bars set in a wall, with a trap behind them. Keep your shield up or sprint past, and do not stop in the line of fire.
Levers | A group of levers must all be in the right position. A sign or glowing text nearby gives the hint, for example "Wake the first and the last".
Pressure plates | Step on every plate in the room. Each lights up for good (until the dungeon resets).
Gates | Some doors open when you clear a room, or when a champion falls.
Key doors | A vault door opens when you right-click it holding the dungeon's key. One key is used up.
Doors close again when the dungeon resets.

A hidden cache, a break-in wall or a sealed alcove is a secret. Walk within about 2.5 blocks the first time and you get "Secret found", 250 coins and 150 Delving XP, once per player per secret. Secrets also add to the Reward Chest (below).
Forgotten Crypt | Crypt Key | boss always, champion 35%, Elites 35%
Spider Hollow | Hollow Key | boss always, Elites 35%
Drowned Temple | Tide Key | boss always, champion 35%, Elites 35%
Dwarven Halls | Thane's Key | champion always, boss always, Elites 35%
Infernal Citadel | Citadel Key | champion always, boss always, Elites 35%
Ruined Citadel | Citadel Crest Key | champion always, boss always, Elites 35%
Catacombs | Ossuary Key | three are needed: one from each Bone Warden, and Elites 35%
Astral Observatory | Observatory Key | champion always, boss always, Elites 35%
You can open the vault before or after the boss.

A champion is a mini-boss on the first floor. It has a boss bar, its own moves, coins and Delving XP, a share of loot, and often the key. It does not leave a Reward Chest. A boss guards the last room and has several phases.

The boss wakes when you walk into its room. A boss nobody fights for 30 seconds goes back to sleep and returns at full health.
It has more health the bigger the party: +60% for each extra player within 32 blocks when it wakes. The party size shows in chat.
A boss that strays more than 28 blocks from its room is teleported home.
Phases are announced at two thirds and one third of its health. New moves unlock with them, and at one third it enrages (faster and harder hitting).
Bosses stronger than vanilla's health cap take less damage instead, and the bar shows the real health.
Moves are announced in the action bar before they land (for example "The Warden raises his blade!"), and slams are marked with a ring on the floor.
Slam | A marked ring, then damage and a launch for everyone inside.
Leap | Jumps at a player and hits everyone near the landing spot.
Volley | Fires arrows, fireballs, web shots or tridents at its target.
Summon | Calls minions around it, up to a limit.
Pull | Drags every player in range towards the boss.
Shockwave | Knocks everyone in range away and hurts them.
Webs | Temporary cobwebs around each nearby player.
Molten | The floor around each player glows, then turns to magma and burns for a few seconds. Keep moving.
Cloud | A lingering poison, wither or blindness cloud.
Ward | The boss takes much less damage for a few seconds. Hold your big attacks.
Heal | The boss heals a share of its health.
Enrage | Once, below one third health: faster and stronger.
Move damage in dungeon pages is in vanilla damage points (1 point is 5 Health on the stats scale), before Defense.
When the boss warns "Fire geysers! Keep moving!" or "The floor glows red-hot", leave the marked spots at once. When it wards, back off and wait, because wards cut damage by 70% to 90%.

Every chest is per player. Each player rolls their own loot from every chest, so nothing is stolen, and what you leave in your copy stays there until the dungeon resets. Each chest also pays coins and Delving XP by its tier and the dungeon's level.
Coins vary by up to 20% either way.
Everyone who hit the boss and is within 64 blocks gets:

coins and Delving XP (each boss's page lists them),
their own roll of the boss's loot table,
the first clear bonus, once per boss (most bosses and champions have one): coins, Combat XP and a "FIRST CLEAR" banner.

Bosses leave a Reward Chest where they fall: a per-player chest, only the party that won can open it. It rolls its table once, plus bonus rolls for how thoroughly you cleared the dungeon: one bonus per 3 packs cleared, one per secret found and two per champion slain, up to 8. It disappears when the dungeon resets. Run through to the boss and you get one roll. Clear the place and you get several.
Bosses also drop enchant tomes, and champions drop lower level ones. Boss tokens are guaranteed.

A used-up dungeon part comes back 72,000 ticks (one real hour, three in-game days) after it was used, but only when no player is within 32 blocks. Bosses, packs, chests and puzzle doors all return. First clears and secrets are per player and stay done.
Bosses drop boss tokens, which you take to the Artisan Bench to craft dungeon gear with no luck needed. The bench's "dungeon" recipes need a Delving level.
Cryptbreaker | 5 | Warden's Sigil, iron, Marrow Shards, Dread Fangs
Warden's Shroud set | 5 | Warden's Sigil, bone, iron, Marrow Shards
Arachne's Fang, Widowsilk Cloak | 12 | Arachne's Eye, string, Brood Silk
Carapace of Arachne set | 12 | Arachne's Eye, string, spider eyes
Tidecaller Blade, Tidemother Pendant | 20 | Tide Pearls, prismarine, Tidescales
Tidemother Regalia set | 20 | Tide Pearls, prismarine, gold
Thane's Hammer, Runeforged set | 20 | Thane's Runes, Dwarven Cogs, Duskquartz
Hellforged armour | 30 | Hellforged Ingots, magma cream (the chestplate also needs a Tyrant's Core)

Each dungeon page lists the exact recipes. The later trophies (the Fallen Crest, the Bonelord's Phylactery and the Star Warden's Core) are not crafted into gear. They are kept for the Void Sigil that summons the Ender Wyrm (one of each trophy, three Sigils per craft). See Ender Wyrm.

Delving (see Delving and Skills overview) has 50 levels. Each level gives +2 Health and +0.25 Magic Find. Its XP comes from dungeon chests, secrets, champions, bosses and discovering dungeons (100 plus 5 per dungeon level). Its talents are Delver's Vigor (+5 Health a rank), Delver's Luck (+1 Magic Find) and Crypt Hardened (+3 Defense).

Bring more than you think. Food, a good ranged weapon, a shield for arrow traps, Water Breathing for the Drowned Temple, fire protection for the Nether, and friends. Boss health goes up by 60% for each extra player, so a party needs more damage, not just more bodies.

Clear packs and find secrets before the boss. The Reward Chest rolls more often.
Kill Elites for the key early, so the vault is ready when you want it.
Do not run at full speed into a room you have not looked at. Packs wake as you come close, and arrow slits cover the corridors.
Dungeons are the main source of dungeon enchant tomes. See Enchanting.

The first dungeon, a two-floor burial complex under forests and plains. The Bone Knight, the Crypt Warden and the gear made from Warden's Sigils.

The Forgotten Crypt is the first dungeon most players clear. It is a sealed two-floor burial complex under forests, plains and meadows, full of skeletons, zombies and the dead of a forgotten order. It is common, easy to find and forgiving, and its boss, the Crypt Warden, drops the Warden's Sigils you need for the first set of dungeon gear. It is a good place to learn how dungeons work.

It generates under any forest, plains, sunflower plains or meadow, about one per 28 by 28 chunks, so it is the most common dungeon.
The entrance is a small stone-brick mausoleum on the surface, with coffins, skulls and candles, and a stair that spirals down. A waystone stands in the corner. Walking near it discovers the dungeon.
Wayshrine chests have a 25% chance of a Forgotten Crypt treasure map.
Floor 1, the Upper Crypt (stone bricks, mossy and cracked):

The mausoleum and its stair.
Three spine halls: long corridors of pillars and coffins, with arrow slits in both long walls and spike plates in the aisle.
The champion arena, where the Bone Knight holds the way down. The gate stays shut until it falls, and arrow slits along the north wall hit anyone who flees.
A stairwell that drops 10 blocks and turns east.
Floor 2, the Ossuary Depths (deepslate tiles and polished blackstone, soul fire):

Three more spine halls.
The Warden's hall, 31 by 15 by 31 blocks: an aisle up to a dais, a sarcophagus, braziers that fire flame traps around the dais, balconies on both sides, and ossuary niches along the wall.
Every spine hall has side doors east and west leading to side rooms. You will meet:
Lever rooms | A gated treasury or cache, opened by levers (see Puzzles).
Guard room | A pack and a chest.
Chapel, library, prison, tomb cell | Packs, chests, decor. The prison has a locked cell with a chest inside.
Embalming room, bone throne, ossuary, catacomb | Packs in big, bony rooms.
Flooded room | A sunken pool with a hidden cache.
Collapsed room | A broken hall with a hidden study.
Packs of 4 to 10, many in two or three waves.
Crypt Archer | skeleton with a bow | everywhere
Bone Knight | armoured skeleton with a sword | floor 1
Restless Dead | zombie with a sword | everywhere
Drowned Dead | drowned with a trident | flooded rooms
Gravecaller, Hollow Wisp | our own mobs | some packs. See Mobs.
Crypt Captain, Wight Captain | Elite zombie and wither skeleton in iron armour | on both floors
Elites carry the Crypt Key, 35% each.

Lever rooms. Two rooms hide their loot behind an iron-bar gate and a row of levers. The sign says what to do. "Wake" means pull the lever on.
The cache. Four levers. "Wake the first and the last. Let the middle two sleep." Pull lever 1 and lever 4 on, and leave 2 and 3 off. It holds a secret cache.
The treasury. Five levers. "Three kings sat, two slept below. Wake the first, the third, the last." Pull levers 1, 3 and 5 on, and leave 2 and 4 off. It holds a rare chest, and a pack with a Crypt Captain guards it.
Arrow slits in the corridors, and spike plates in the aisles of the spine halls.
Flame traps around the Warden's dais. Do not stand on the braziers.
Secrets (250 coins and 150 Delving XP each, once): Sealed Burial, Hidden Burial, Sleepers' Cache, Drowned Cache, Hidden Study and the Warden's Vault.
Level 16, 1,200 health, a skeleton in iron armour, scaled 1.4 times. Melee 10.
Slam | every 10 s | A 5 block ring, damage 10 after a short wind-up.
Summon | every 19 s | 2 Crypt Archers and a Restless Dead (level 15), up to 4 alive.
Blink | every 14 s | Teleports behind you.

Pays: 800 to 1,200 coins and 400 Delving XP; first clear 1,500 coins and 500 Combat XP. Loot: 50% a Warden's Sigil (1 to 2), 35% a Crypt Key, 80% Runic Dust, 2 to 5 Valor Marks, iron and bones. Tomes: Hallowed Edge II (12%), Soul Siphon I, Aegis II and Vitality II (8% each).

Level 18, 4,500 health (plus 60% for each extra player), a giant wither skeleton in netherite armour, scaled 1.6 times. Melee 14. It says "Who disturbs the Warden's rest? The dead keep their oaths." Phases are announced at two thirds and one third health. Move damage is in vanilla points (1 point is 5 Health).
Slam | start | every 11 s | A 6 block ring: "the floor cracks". Damage 14 after a 1.2 s wind-up, and a launch.
Summon | start | every 21 s | 3 Crypt Archers and 2 Restless Dead (level 17), up to 6 alive.
Blink | start | every 15 s | Vanishes and appears behind you.
Shockwave | start | every 17 s | A 9 block ring, damage 10, pushes you away.
Soulfire volley | below 66% | every 13 s | 3 fireballs, damage 8 each, spread out.
Spectral plate (ward) | below 50% | every 35 s | Takes 85% less damage for 7 seconds.
Enrage | below 33% | once | 33% faster and 35% more damage.

Fight it in the aisle with your back to a pillar so the archers cannot flank you, and kill the summons on the spot. When "Spectral plate hardens around the Warden", stop swinging, back off and wait about 7 seconds. In the last third, leave the 6 block slam ring as soon as it flashes.
The Warden's kill (each player who hit it):

coins 3,000 to 4,500 and 1,500 Delving XP,
2 to 4 Warden's Sigils, a Crypt Key, 6 to 14 emeralds, 4 to 10 gold, 3 to 6 Runic Dust (90%), 3 to 6 Valor Marks,
a 25% chance of a Nightmare Core,
15% each of the Cryptbreaker and the four Warden's Shroud pieces,
a 40% chance of a Spider Hollow map,
tomes: Hallowed Edge III (30%) and V (10%), Soul Siphon II (15%), Aegis III (15%), Vitality III (12%) and V (8%).

A two-floor spider nest under dark forests and pale gardens. The Silk Matron, Queen Arachne, and the gear made from Arachne's Eyes.

Spider Hollow is a spider nest dug under dark forests and pale gardens: web-choked tunnels, glowing grottoes, silk bridges over underground lakes, and a queen at the bottom. It is the second dungeon, a step up from the Forgotten Crypt, and it asks you to deal with webs, poison and swarms. Its boss, Queen Arachne, drops Arachne's Eyes for a poison sword, a dodge cloak and the Carapace set.

It generates under dark forests and pale gardens, about one per 18 by 18 chunks, kept 10 chunks from Forgotten Crypts.
The entrance is a sinkhole in the forest floor with a waystone beside it.
The Crypt Warden has a 40% chance of dropping a treasure map to Spider Hollow.
The tunnels are carved into rock, with moss, tuff and calcite on floor 1 and deepslate, basalt and sculk on floor 2.

The sinkhole and a shaft down.
Three spine halls of webbed tunnels, 21 blocks deep each.
The champion nest, where the Silk Matron waits behind a door plug.

Side doors off every hall lead to themed chambers: egg chambers, brood nests, cocoon galleries, glimmer and mushroom grottoes, an underground lake, silk bridges, venom pools, collapsed mines, bone pits, a web maze and the plate puzzle room. Most hold a pack and a chest. Silk bridges have spike traps, venom pools have poison clouds, and the web maze has spike traps and a chest at its heart.

A flooded two-floor temple on the ocean floor. The Abyssal Herald, the Tidemother, and the gear made from Tide Pearls.

The Drowned Temple is a vast sunken temple of an older sea-faith, built on the ocean floor and flooded to the rafters. It has two floors of prismarine and sandstone halls, drowned guards with tridents, and a goddess of the deep at the bottom. It is the third dungeon, and the first where the environment is part of the fight: you swim, you fight in water, and you hunt for the air pockets. Its boss, the Tidemother, drops the Tide Pearls for the Tidecaller Blade and the Tidemother Regalia.
Mob levels | 26 to 28 (floor 1), 29 to 32 (floor 2), Elites 3 higher

Almost everything is underwater, doorways included. Bring Water Breathing and plenty of light. Air pockets (shrines, ledges, the champion hall and the sanctum) let you breathe, but do not rely on them.

It generates on the ocean floor in oceans of any depth, and in cold and warm oceans, but not in frozen oceans. One per 32 by 32 chunks.
The entrance is an open forecourt of smooth sandstone and sea lanterns on the sea floor, with a waystone and coral mounds. Dive and look for the glow.
Queen Arachne has a 40% chance of dropping a treasure map to the Temple.

A flooded descent, a ramp 10 blocks down that turns the temple a quarter turn.

Three more spine halls, including vent galleries and sculk halls.

A ruined dwarven city under the mountains, reached by a long stairwell. The Forgeguard, the Iron Thane, and the Runeforged gear.

The Dwarven Halls are a ruined dwarven city, built into the rock under mountains, hills and forests. You enter through a broken stone gate on a hillside and walk down a very long spiral stair into forge halls, barracks, rail stations and vaults lit by glowing runes. Lost Miners and clockwork Constructs still guard it. It is the fourth dungeon, and its boss, the Iron Thane, drops the runes for the Thane's Hammer and the Runeforged set.
Mob levels | 32 to 36 (Upper Halls), 36 to 41 (Deep Forge)

It generates under mountains, hills, forests, windswept hills and forests, and stony peaks, about one per 40 by 40 chunks, and never within 8 chunks of a Spider Hollow.
The entrance is the ruined Dwarven Gate: a carved deepslate doorway in a hillside with braziers, a collapsed statue and a waystone. Walking near it discovers the dungeon.
Abandoned Mine Camps (small camps in caves, guarded by Lost Miners) have a 15% chance of a Dwarven Halls treasure map in their chests.
The same dwarven stone shows up in the Dwarven Halls layer of the caves (y -40 to -20), but the dungeon itself is a separate structure. See The Deep.
The halls run deep, so budget for a long walk and a long climb out. Use the waystone at the gate to come back.
The surface and the stairwell. From the gate, a square-spiral stair of about 76 blocks goes down, with landings that hold packs, chests and arrow traps. It leaves through an east door at the bottom.

The Infernal Citadel is a blackstone fortress in the Nether, on stilts over the lava sea or built into a cliff. Its halls are lined with polished blackstone bricks, gilded blackstone, nether bricks and soul-fire braziers, with lava falls behind iron bars. It is the fifth dungeon and the first one outside the overworld. Its boss, the Magma Tyrant, drops the Tyrant's Core and the Hellforged scrap you need for the fire-proof Hellforged armour.

Lava is everywhere. Fire resistance, or fire immunity from the Hellforged armour, will save your life. Check your gear before you go through the Nether portal. See The Nether.

It generates in the Nether wastes, basalt deltas and soul sand valleys, and in the new Nether biomes (Ember Forest, Bone Sea and Obsidian Spires). One per 44 by 44 chunks, so it is rare, and never within 8 chunks of a vanilla fortress or bastion.

The Ruined Citadel is a castle sunk into the mountain peaks: a broken gatehouse on the slope, then three floors of sunken courtyards, libraries, chapels and a throne room under the rock. Armoured zombies, skeleton knights and castle guards still hold it. It is the sixth dungeon, and the first with three floors. Its boss, the Fallen Knight, drops the Fallen Crest, a trophy for the Void Sigil that summons the Ender Wyrm, plus top-tier materials and a Reward Chest.

It generates in the mountains: frozen peaks, jagged peaks, stony peaks, snowy slopes, groves and windswept hills (including gravelly hills). One per 56 by 56 chunks, and never within 10 chunks of the Dwarven Halls.
The entrance is a ruined gatehouse built into the slope: two broken towers, a gate arch, a plaza with banners on poles, a fallen statue and a waystone. Walking near it discovers the dungeon.
The questline asks you to find it. See Quests and journal.
From the gatehouse a tunnel leads into a stairwell with two landings (each with a pack, chests and an arrow trap), and the castle runs under the mountain.

A sealed labyrinth of crypts under the Magma Rifts. Hunt three Bone Wardens for their keys, open the tomb and face the Bonelord.

The Catacombs are a labyrinth of crypts, buried in the deep rock of the overworld with no door on the surface. You find the sealed stair, dig your way in, and hunt through mazes, ossuaries and lever halls for three Ossuary Keys. Each is held by a Bone Warden, a giant skeleton. The keys open the three bone doors of the inner tomb, where the Bonelord waits. It is the seventh dungeon, and it asks for a bit of everything: puzzles, traps, a key hunt and one big boss.
Champions | Three Bone Wardens (level 60, 15,000 health each)

It generates anywhere in the overworld, very rarely (one per 64 by 64 chunks), and the whole structure lies between about y -59 and y -36, in the Magma Rifts layer. See The Deep.
There is no surface part and no treasure map. The easiest way to find it is the questline: track "The Catacombs" in your journal and a waypoint points at the nearest one within 100 chunks. See Quests and journal.
The entrance is a sealed stair: solid rock around a square-spiral stair of 18 blocks. Its top is a small sealed bone chamber at about y -41, with a sign reading "SEALED. The dead keep their own counsel.", candles, skulls, a chest, and a cracked wall. Dig down to it and break through the cracked wall. Unlike the other dungeons, there is no waystone here.
Digging into the Magma Rifts is dangerous on its own: lava pools and Fire Beetles. Bring fire protection and a way to escape. See Mobs.
The Catacombs are one labyrinth with no floors. Everything is a stage on the way to the tomb.

The entrance stair, with two landings (packs and an arrow trap), then out to the south.
Stage 1 and stage 2 of the spine, each 21 blocks deep. Each stage is either a maze (6 by 5 cells with loops, dead-end chests and packs, traps) or a hall: a crypt hall, an ossuary hall, a lever hall or a plate hall. The lever and plate halls shut the spine with a bone grate until the puzzle is solved. Every spine piece has a west and an east door.
The tomb gate: a hall of three bone doors in a row.
The Bonelord's Crypt, 31 by 18 by 31 blocks, with bone arches, a throne and a hoard alcove that opens when he dies.

Bone Warden chambers. The west and east doors of stage 1, and the west door of stage 2, lead to a chamber with a Bone Warden. Each drops exactly one Ossuary Key.
The side rooms off the east door of stage 2: an ossuary, a bone pit, sarcophagi, a trap gallery, a shrine, a lever vault, a plate vault and a charnel house.
Lanes: crossroads, tees and straight tunnels cut from solid stone, ending in leaf rooms (urns, a cache, a grave).

The tomb needs three Ossuary Keys, one per bone door. A door uses up one key per click, so the gate is three doors in a row, labelled "SEAL 1", "SEAL 2" and "SEAL 3": "Press an Ossuary Key to the bone."

Each of the three Bone Wardens drops one.

A purpur and glass observatory on the outer End islands. The Astral Sentinel, the Star Warden and the Star Warden's Core.

The Astral Observatory is the last dungeon: a purpur and glass observatory on the outer End islands, with star-map murals, telescopes, glass roofs and end rods. You climb through the Lower Halls past the Astral Sentinel, up to the Star Deck, and into the Dome where the Star Warden keeps the sky. It is the hardest fight in the game short of the Ender Wyrm, and its boss drops the Star Warden's Core and the Astral Shards that go into the Void Sigils that summon the Wyrm.
Mob levels | 60 to 63 (Lower Halls), 63 to 65 (Star Deck)

It generates on the outer End islands: the End highlands, midlands and barrens, and the new Void Gardens, Shattered Isles and Astral Fields biomes. One per 26 by 26 chunks, and never within 6 chunks of an End city. The main island does not have one. See The End.
Track "The Astral Observatory" in your journal and a waypoint points at the nearest one. See Quests and journal.
The first floor stands on purpur stilts, on the island or over the void, at about y 68. The second floats on a thin hull above it.
The entrance is the Courtyard: a terrace on stilts with a waystone, a telescope and a gate 7 blocks wide, leading to an atrium under a glass roof.
The first floor stands on stilts, sometimes over the void, and the End has no safe ground below it. Bring a way to stop a fall (blocks, slow falling) and be careful at the edges.

The Ascent: a tower with two switchback flights of purpur stairs, 20 blocks up. It leaves by its east wall.
Side rooms: a telescope room, a map room, a lens workshop and the astronomer's quarters (with a cache). Small rooms: a closet, a stargazer's nook (a cache) and a guard post.

The Star Warden's Dome, 35 by 28 by 35 blocks: a glass roof and windows, a star chart inlaid in the floor, and the great telescope in a back alcove. A key-door vault and a hoard nook (which opens when the Warden dies) are here.
There are no lever or plate puzzles. The doors are the champion's bar plug, the vault's key door and the hoard door.
Astral Acolyte | enderman. Some are Elites.
Mad Astronomer | witch. Some are Elites.
Elites carry the Observatory Key (35%). Arrow slits shoot at you in many halls (13 damage on floor 1, 16 on floor 2).
Shulker bullets levitate you, so deal with Star Sentinels early. Do not look at an Astral Acolyte until you are ready to fight it: like any enderman, it attacks when you look it in the eyes.
Level 62, 24,000 health, an enderman scaled 1.8 times with 85% knockback resistance. Melee 40. "The sky is closed to the unlettered."
Flicker (blink) | every 8 s | Vanishes and appears behind you.
Long arm (slam) | every 11.5 s | 6 block ring, damage 38, launches you.
Shell of light (ward) | below 50%, every 40 s | Takes 75% less damage for 5 seconds.
Summon | every 24 s | 3 Void Mites (level 62), up to 4 alive.

Pays: 14,000 to 18,000 coins and 6,000 Delving XP; first clear 16,000 coins and 7,000 Combat XP. It always drops an Observatory Key and 3 to 6 Astral Shards. Also ender pearls, ender eyes, shulker shells, 25% a Dread Crystal, 35% an Elite Trophy, 8% a Nightmare Core. Tomes: Cleave III and Bloodthirst III (8% each), Steadfast III (6%), Vitality IV (8%).

Level 64, 60,000 health (+60% per extra player), an enderman scaled 2.5 times. Melee 56. "The great lens swings round and the dome goes dark. 'I keep the sky.'" Move damage is in vanilla points (1 point is 5 Health).
Step between stars (blink) | start | every 7 s | Appears behind you.
Starlight volley | start | every 10.5 s | 6 arrows, damage 22.
Collapsed-star fist (slam) | start | every 11.5 s | 8 block ring, damage 52, launches you.
Black hole (pull) | below 66% | every 18 s | Drags everyone within 18 blocks into his palm, hard.
Summon | below 66% | every 23 s | 2 Astral Acolytes and 3 Void Mites (level 62), up to 6 alive.
Shell of starlight (ward) | below 50% | every 45 s | Takes 80% less damage for 6 seconds.
Starlight ring (shockwave) | below 33% | every 15 s | 12 block ring, damage 40, a huge push.
Enrage | below 33% | once | 38% faster and 40% more damage.
At two thirds "the lenses align" and the Warden calls his acolytes. At one third "the dome cracks and starlight pours in".

Expect the Warden at your back every 7 seconds. The black hole drags you towards him, so be ready to leave the 8 block slam ring straight after. Spend your burst when the ward drops, and kill the Mites quickly.
The Star Warden's kill (each player who hit it):

coins 60,000 to 80,000 and 28,000 Delving XP,
a Star Warden's Core (and a 25% chance of a second), an Observatory Key and 8 to 14 Astral Shards,

tomes: Reaper's Mark IV (12%) and V (5%), Bloodthirst IV (12%) and V (5%), Cleave V (15%), Vitality VI (15%) and Soulrend III (4%).
First clear: 110,000 coins and 36,000 Combat XP.

The Reward Chest rolls 5 to 7 times for Astral Shards, ender eyes, shulker shells, echo shards, Dread Crystals, Heartstones and more, with a 22% Nightmare Core, a 35% chance of 1 to 2 Dread Fangs, a 4% Golden Pet Egg and a 12% pup or mole egg.
The vault (in the Dome, one Observatory Key) pays about 6,400 coins and 1,600 Delving XP. The vault also has a 2% chance of an elytra.

The Star Warden's Core sells for 11,000 coins. Astral Shards are also dropped by Astral Crystals, which grow in the Astral Fields. They go into the Void Sigil that summons the Ender Wyrm. See Ender Wyrm.

Treat it as an end-game raid: your best gear, food and healing, and a stack of blocks for the void. The Warden's health rises by 60% for each extra player in the room, so bring people who add real damage.

Do not skip the Sentinel. It always drops the Observatory Key that opens the vault.
Clear packs and find secrets for the Reward Chest bonus.

The survival world versus the Skyhaven hub, the Wildgate, /survival and /hub, what is protected where, and what happens when you die.

SkyRPG has two places to be. Skyhaven is the safe hub where everyone spawns, shops and talks to NPCs. The survival world is the normal Minecraft world (Overworld, Nether and End) where you mine, fight, farm and explore. Knowing how the two fit together tells you where you are safe, where you are not, and what you keep when things go wrong.
What it is | A floating town in its own void dimension | The Overworld, the Nether and the End
Spawn | You arrive at the hub on first join | Reached through the Wildgate or /survival
Building and breaking | Not allowed (creative mode excepted) | Allowed, as in normal Minecraft
Fighting and damage | Nothing can hurt you, and you cannot hit anything | Everything can hurt you
Hunger | Your food bar stays full | Normal
Mobs | None | Levelled monsters, Elites, bosses, danger regions
The hub holds the trade Masters, the shops, the Artisan Bench and the bank. See Skyhaven for the town itself.
The Wildgate is the glowing ring on the south islet of Skyhaven. Walk into it and you are sent to the survival world. There is no button to press and no cost.

You return to exactly where you left: the same dimension, coordinates and facing. If you left from the Nether, you come back to the Nether.
If you have never left the hub before, you arrive at the survival world's spawn, on the surface.
You can also skip the walk with commands:
/hub | Takes you to Skyhaven from anywhere. Your survival position is remembered.
/survival | Takes you back to where you left the survival world. Only works while you are in the hub.

In combat (see Combat basics) they are refused, and the message shows how many seconds are left.
Otherwise you must stand still for 5 seconds. The action bar counts down, a ring of sparkles closes in around your feet and a tick sounds each second, then you go.
The warm-up is cancelled if you move more than about a third of a block, take damage, get into a fight or change dimension. Dying or logging out cancels it too.
Type the command again during the warm-up to cancel it yourself.
Creative and spectator players skip the wait, so builders can move freely.
Walking through the Wildgate has no warm-up.

/hub does not cost anything and works from the Nether and End too. If you are low on health and a long way from a waystone, it is the quickest way out. /survival puts you straight back where you stood.
Using a waystone to return to Skyhaven does the same thing as /hub. See Waystones and Travel.
The hub is kept exactly as built. Unless you are in creative mode:

You cannot break or place blocks, use buckets, or spawn mobs with eggs.
You cannot attack anything, and nothing takes damage (the void is the one exception).
Item frames, paintings and armour stands cannot be changed.
Blocks cannot be used unless they are on the hub's "usable" list. Doors, buttons and similar things work.
Farmland cannot be trampled.
Your hunger and saturation are topped up while you stand there.
If you fall off the island below the void line (y 0), you are put back at the spawn point.
There is no land protection. You can build, dig and place planters anywhere outside the hub, and so can the monsters. A few things are deliberately safe:

Waystones survive explosions, and breaking one with a pickaxe gives you the waystone as an item to place somewhere else (everyone attuned follows it). Skyhaven's and the dungeon entrances' waystones are fixed in place. See Waystones and Travel.
Chests inside dungeons are per player, so nobody can steal your loot.
Mounts that would die are knocked out and fly home instead. See Mounts.
Every hostile mob in the survival world gets a level when it spawns:
Surface | 1 near world spawn, plus 1 for every 120 blocks you travel out, up to 30

Each level above 1 adds 8% health and 5% damage. Danger regions, the Deep and the Blood Moon then add extra levels on top of the cap, so a Shattered Highlands monster can reach level 50 on the surface alone and level 60 under a Blood Moon.
Mobs you spawn with eggs or commands have no level.
Distance from the world spawn is the main thing that makes the surface harder. A trip of 3,600 blocks puts you at level 30 on ordinary ground, before any region bonus.
The world spawn point is Skyhaven. If you die and have no bed or respawn anchor set, you wake up in the hub. If you slept in a bed in the survival world, you respawn there as in vanilla Minecraft.
What you keep when you die (it is stored on you, not in your inventory):

Your coin purse and your bank
Your accessories (the Amulet, Cloak, Belt and Bracers slots) and your backpacks
Your mounts and their stable
Your slayer progress, titles and enchanting codex

Everything else in your main inventory and armour follows the server's normal death rules. I could not check the server's keepInventory setting from the game's files, so ask the staff if you need to know.
A red "Last death" waypoint is added to your map where you died, so you can walk back and collect what dropped. See Waypoints and HUD and Minimap.

Where waystones and Wayshrines are, how to attune and travel, what it costs, and the other ways to get around.

A waystone is a stone you can attune to and later travel back to. Once you have attuned to a few, you can jump between them, or home to Skyhaven, for a small number of XP levels. They are the backbone of long trips in the survival world, so it pays to attune to every one you walk past. You can also pick them up and move them, rename them and craft new ones to build a network of your own.
Waystones stand in three kinds of place:

Wayshrines: small ruined shrines of mossy stone brick with a waystone on a dais, candles, broken pillars and a chest. They generate in forests, taiga, savanna, plains, sunflower plains, meadows, snowy plains, deserts, birch forests and cherry groves.
Villages: the first time a village's bell area loads, a waystone is placed two to four blocks from the bell.
Dungeons: every dungeon entrance has one, including the Infernal Citadel in the Nether and the Astral Observatory in the End.
Skyhaven has one as well, just left of the spawn point.

Wayshrine and village waystones can be picked up and moved (see Moving and building your own). The waystone in Skyhaven and the ones at dungeon entrances are fixed: they anchor the dungeon, so they cannot be taken away.

Wayshrines are common: the world is cut into 24-chunk (384-block) squares and each can hold one, at least 8 chunks from the next. The Shrine Chest in each holds 2 to 4 stacks from bread, apples, cooked beef, carrots, torches, arrows, string, sticks and iron nuggets, plus 1 to 2 Runic Dust and a map. Like dungeon chests, it is rolled per player, so everyone who visits gets their own loot.

Walk up to a waystone and right-click it.
The first time, it lights up (a lit waystone glows brighter), you get a WAYSTONE ATTUNED banner with its name, and it is added to your list and to your map.
Right-click it again to open the travel menu.
Waystones get an automatic name: the dungeon it guards, <Name> Village, or a made-up place name followed by the biome, for example "Ravenwatch · Taiga".
A waystone's name is shown in the travel list, on the world map and in the banner when you attune. See Renaming to change it.

Mine a waystone with any pickaxe. It takes a few seconds (a wooden pickaxe is slow, an iron or better one is quick) and it comes off as a Waystone item named after the stone, which remembers exactly which waystone it was. Nothing else will do: without a pickaxe the break is refused.

Place it again anywhere and it is the same waystone, in its new spot. Everyone who was attuned to it stays attuned, and from then on their travel list, map and costs point at the new place. It keeps its name and its glow.
While you carry it, nobody can travel to it (it is greyed out of their list, and it comes back on its own once it is placed). Players stay attuned the whole time.
The item will not despawn or burn up, but if it falls into the void or you lose it the waystone is lost with it. A stack can never hold two: each carried waystone is its own item.
Placing a waystone attunes you to it straight away.
You cannot copy a waystone: if the waystone an item remembers already stands somewhere, a second placement makes a brand-new, separate waystone instead.

Skyhaven's waystone, and every dungeon entrance waystone. Swinging at one says so on the action bar.
Anything in Skyhaven itself, where nothing can be broken.

What cannot destroy a waystone: explosions (creepers, TNT, beds in the Nether and so on) leave it standing, pistons will not push it, and the Wither and the Ender Dragon cannot break it. If anything else does take one away, such as a command, it drops as its item rather than vanishing.
Craft a Waystone at the Artisan Bench (General tab). It needs Mining 8:

Place it where you need it: it gets an automatic name (a made-up place and the biome), you are attuned to it and you are listed as its owner. Travel between your own waystones costs the same XP as any other.
Open the waystone's menu and click Rename at the top right, type a name of up to 24 characters and press Enter. The new name shows to everyone, in the travel list and on the map.

The player who placed a waystone (or crafted and placed it) is its owner and the only one who can rename it.
Generated waystones (wayshrines, villages, dungeon entrances) can be renamed by anyone who is attuned to them.
Skyhaven's waystone keeps its name.
A carried waystone can be renamed in an anvil; the new name is used when you place it.
A name tag with a name on it, used on the waystone, also renames it (and is used up), under the same rules.
The menu lists Skyhaven first (outside the hub) and then every waystone you have attuned to, with its world, distance and coordinates. Click one to go.
From Skyhaven to any attuned waystone | 2 XP levels
Waystone to waystone, same dimension | 1 XP level per 1,000 blocks of distance, plus 1 (maximum 5)
Waystone to waystone, between dimensions | 4 XP levels
That means anything under 1,000 blocks costs 1 level, 1,000 to 1,999 costs 2, and so on up to the 5-level cap at 4,000 blocks. Creative players travel for free.
You land on a free spot next to the destination waystone, facing it. A few rules:

You must still be within 6 blocks of the waystone when you click, and you need enough XP levels.
If a waystone is being carried, it is left out of the list until somebody places it again. If it no longer exists, you get "That waystone is gone" and it drops off your list.
Destinations are saved on you, so your list follows you between worlds and dimensions.
Choosing a destination does not take you there at once:

In combat the trip is refused (see Combat basics).
Otherwise you stand still for 5 seconds with a countdown in the action bar, a ring of sparkles and a tick each second. Moving more than about a third of a block, taking damage or getting into a fight cancels it, and you keep your XP.
The XP levels are paid when you arrive, not when you click.
Creative players skip the wait. Going back to Skyhaven has the same one 5 second wait, not two.
Attune to a waystone before you head into a danger region or dungeon. When your health is low, the trip home costs at most 5 levels, which is far cheaper than a death run back through monsters.
Waystone icons on the world map can be clicked for Track and Share in chat, which makes it easy to tell a friend where to meet you. See Waypoints.
/hub and /survival | Free, with the same 5 second warm-up and no use in combat. /hub goes to Skyhaven from anywhere, /survival returns you to where you left. See The Survival World.
Griffin mounts | Tame a griffin in the Shattered Highlands and ride it. Flight uses stamina that refills on the ground. See Mounts.
Waypoints | Not a teleport, but they point the way. Track a waypoint and a marker, a ribbon and an arrow guide you. See Waypoints.
Vanilla routes | Boats, minecarts (Abandoned Mine Camps leave rails behind), ender pearls and Nether portals all still work.
Dungeon maps | Treasure maps from bosses and chests point to the next dungeon.

Load a schematic or a village house, place its hologram, deliver the materials and watch it build itself from the ground up.

The Builder Station turns a blueprint into a real build. Pick a blueprint (one of Minecraft's village houses, or your own schematic file), place its glowing hologram where you want it, deliver the materials it lists, press Build, and it rises from the ground up, layer by layer, in front of you.
Craft a Builder Station at the Artisan Bench (General tab). It needs Foraging 5:
Place it anywhere in the survival world. Its crystal lens faces you, and new blueprints first appear behind it. Right-click it to open the builder menu. Stations don't work in Skyhaven.
Press Choose blueprint (or Blueprint... later). The picker has two tabs and two views:

Library: every blueprint on the server. Minecraft's own buildings are always there: the houses and town centres of all five village types (plains, taiga, savanna, desert, snowy), the igloo, the pillager outpost watchtower and the ruined portals. Schematics anyone has uploaded are listed first, with who uploaded them. You can delete your own uploads.
My schematics: the schematic files on your computer, in the schematics folder of your game (the same folder Litematica uses; Open folder opens it). Clicking one uploads it to the server's library and loads it. Uploaded blueprints are shared with everyone on the server.
Cards shows each blueprint as a card with a turning 3D preview and its size underneath. List is a compact list. Both have a search box.
Picking a blueprint closes the menu and goes straight to placing it in the world (below).

Supported files: .litematic (Litematica, every region), .schem (WorldEdit / Sponge, versions 1 to 3) and .nbt (vanilla structure block files). Old MCEdit .schematic files are not supported: save them as .litematic or .schem first. A blueprint can be at most 128 blocks on each side, 120,000 blocks in all, and the file at most 2 MB. Files from older Minecraft versions are updated as they load, and the card says why a file can't be read before you upload it.

A blueprint is placed in the world, not in a menu. Its hologram (see-through blocks with a cyan outline) follows where you aim: the side nearest you sits on the block you look at and the build stretches away from you. Walk around and aim until it's where you want it. A strip at the bottom of the screen shows the keys:
Aim | Move it (it follows the block you look at, up to 64 blocks away)
Scroll, or R | Turn it 90° (Shift+R: the other way)
↑ ↓ ← → | Nudge it one block away, towards you, left or right of where you look (Shift: 5 blocks). This locks it in place
Page Up / Page Down, or Shift+scroll | Raise or lower it
G | Lock it in place, or let it follow your aim again
Left-click, or Enter | Place it here
Esc, Backspace, or right-click | Cancel (it goes back to where it was)

While you place, clicks and those keys only move the hologram: you won't break or place blocks by accident. It turns red when it's more than 64 blocks from its station (or would cover the station), and then it can't be placed. To move a placed blueprint later, sneak + right-click the station (whatever you're holding), or open it and press Move in world. Moving one that's already placed starts locked where it is, so the arrow keys fine-tune it; press G to make it follow your aim again. You can place it from anywhere up to 64 blocks from the station.
Once placed, everyone nearby sees the hologram. Blocks that are already in place disappear from it, and blocks that are in the way glow red. Hologram on/off in the menu hides it.
The left side of the menu shows the blueprint four ways:

3D: a model that turns by itself; drag (or scroll) to turn it yourself. Real shows every block as it looks (torches, flowers, glass, water); Simple shows plain coloured cubes.
Top: seen from above, north up, higher blocks brighter.
Side: seen from the south.
Layers: one layer at a time; scroll for the others. Hover a block to see what it is.
While it builds, the parts not built yet are faded (in 3D they're cyan hologram), and the Layers view follows the layer being built.
The right side lists everything the build needs, how much you've delivered and a bar for each. Blocks already standing in the right place don't need materials.

Deliver all takes everything the build still needs from your inventory and backpacks (never more than it needs). Click one material to deliver just that one.
List or Grid: a list with names and bars, or a grid of bigger icons that fits many more at once.
Each material shows how many you carry (green: enough for what's missing, gold: some). Hover one for the details; Deliver all's tooltip says how much you could deliver now.
Shift-click a row, or press Take back, to get delivered materials back (not while it is building).
In creative mode delivering is free.
Anyone can open the station and deliver, so friends can chip in. The menu shows who delivered how much ("Delivered by").

Most blocks cost their own item. Doors, beds and tall plants are paid for once; double slabs cost two slabs; candles, sea pickles, turtle eggs, petals and snow layers cost one item per piece.
Crops cost their seeds (wheat seeds, carrots, potatoes...), and a potted plant costs a flower pot plus the plant.
Grass blocks, dirt paths, farmland and mycelium take plain dirt.
Water and lava sources cost a full bucket; the empty bucket comes back in the leftovers.
Some blocks are never built and are left out of the cost ("skipped" in the menu): spawners, bedrock, barriers, portals and portal frames, command and structure blocks, budding amethyst, infested blocks, player heads, the dragon egg, and blocks from other mods.
Chests, barrels and the like are built empty. Signs keep their text, banners their patterns and heads their owner.
When everything is delivered the status turns READY TO BUILD. Press Build (or Enter). The menu closes so you can watch.

The station's lens lights up and the build goes up layer by layer from the ground, sweeping out from the station, with a beam from the lens to each new block and a glowing plane at the layer being built. Each layer is cleared first, then its solid blocks go in, then the things that hang on them (torches, doors, carpets). It takes its time so you can watch it: about 12 seconds plus a little per block and per layer, with a short rest after each layer. A small village house takes about 45 seconds, bigger builds a few minutes (3 at most).

Everyone within 64 blocks gets a build panel in the bottom-right corner: a big 3D model of the build (built part in colour, the rest as hologram), its name, a progress bar, the layer, blocks placed and about how long is left. It says FINISHED! when it's done.
The 3D previews (blueprint cards, the station, the build panel) have two settings under K menu → Settings → Builder:

Preview style: Real (default) or Simple. The Real / Simple button in the station and the blueprint picker switches it too.
Preview quality: Low, Medium or High (default). Lower is lighter on slower computers.

Stand clear: the build waits for anyone standing where a block goes.
If it runs out of a material (someone took a block away, for example), it pauses and says what it's waiting for. Deliver more and it carries on.
Stop pauses the build. Press Build again later and it carries on where it left off.
When it's done you get a burst of fireworks and a message. Build again plans the same blueprint again (move it first); New blueprint picks another.

With Clear site on (the default), blocks that are in the way are removed as the layers go up, so the build comes out exactly like the blueprint, air included. What they drop goes to the station's leftovers, but only blocks you could break by hand drop anything: dirt, sand, plants, logs and planks come back, while stone and ores just vanish. Items inside containers that are cleared away go to the leftovers too. Bedrock and other unbreakable blocks are never touched.
With Clear site off, nothing that's already there is touched: blocks in the way are simply left out of the build.
Press Collect leftovers to take them.
Break the station with an axe to move it. Everything delivered to it, and its leftovers, drop on the spot. A build in progress stops.

Put a schematic you made with Litematica (or downloaded) in your schematics folder and it shows up under My schematics, with a preview, right away.
Use Turn before moving: it turns about the middle, so the build stays roughly where you put it.
Turn Clear site off when building into an existing build, so nothing of yours is removed.
Corrupted patches of the Overworld with much stronger monsters. Where they are, the six types, what lives there and what they drop.

A danger region is a big patch of the Overworld where the land itself is corrupted and the monsters are many levels stronger than the ground around them. Regions show red on your map, with the region's name at the centre. They are the best place to find regional materials (essences) and the rare Dread Crystal, and the best way to get killed if you wander in unprepared.
Regions come from the world seed, so every world is different, but the rules are the same:

The Overworld is cut into 768-block cells. Each cell has a 24% chance to hold one region. That works out to roughly one region every 1,600 blocks.
The centre falls in the middle half of its cell. The region's radius is 150 to 230 blocks, and its edge wobbles, so every region is a different blob rather than a circle.
The biome at the centre decides the type. If no type wants that biome (oceans, for example), the cell has no region.
Nothing is placed within 450 blocks of the world spawn.
Where two regions overlap, you count as being in the one you are deeper inside.
The Ashen Wastes | savanna, badlands, desert | 4 skulls | +18
Frostgrave | snowy plains, snowy taiga, ice spikes, groves, snowy slopes | 4 skulls | +18
The Mire | swamps, mangrove swamps | 2 skulls | +12
The Haunted Moors | plains, sunflower plains, meadows | 3 skulls | +16
The Shattered Highlands | stony, jagged and frozen peaks, windswept hills, gravelly hills and forest | 4 skulls | +20
A snowy taiga can be either Blightlands or Frostgrave (Blightlands is slightly more likely).

Regions are drawn on the world map and minimap as a red wash, strongest at the border, with a marker at the centre. Hover the marker to see its danger.
/region lists the regions near you, with distance, in the form "Frostgrave ☠☠☠☠ at x, z (r 190, 640 blocks away)". Anyone can use it. Ops have /region list (3,000 blocks) and /region nearest <type> (30,000 blocks).
When you cross the border, you get a red title with the region's name, its skulls and "Monsters +N levels", and a low sound. A message tells you when you leave.
Inside, particles drift around you (crimson spores, ash, snowflakes, spores or clouds) and the fog changes colour.
The monster bonus is added on top of ordinary distance levels, and it is not capped at 50. Far from spawn, a Shattered Highlands monster is level 50, and a Blood Moon adds 10 more.

The land. Chunks generated after the update are rewritten: ground, trees and plants change to the region's own blocks, from 40 blocks above the ground to 4 below, and the edge frays over 12 blocks. Chunks that existed before keep their old look, but the danger still applies.
The monsters. Every monster that spawns inside gets the region's level bonus, natural or not.
Roaming groups. Every 3 seconds, near each survival player inside, the region may spawn a group from its own list 18 to 36 blocks away, up to a cap of 8 or 9 of its monsters within 48 blocks. These can despawn normally.
Drops. Monsters killed by a player inside roll the region's drops: its essence (35%, 1 to 2) and a Dread Crystal (0.8%). Farmed mobs do not drop them.
A heart. The centre holds a shrine and a boss. See Region Hearts.
Blight Essence | Uncommon |  | 60 coins | Mined from Blight Crystal; Dropped by The Blight Lord
Cinder Essence | Uncommon |  | 60 coins | Dropped by The Ash Colossus; Dropped by monsters in The Ashen Wastes
Frost Essence | Uncommon |  | 60 coins | Dropped by The Frost Revenant King; Dropped by monsters in Frostgrave
Mire Essence | Uncommon |  | 60 coins | Dropped by The Bog Mother; Dropped by monsters in The Mire
Ectoplasm | Uncommon |  | 60 coins | Dropped by The Lantern Wraith; Dropped by monsters in The Haunted Moors
Gale Essence | Uncommon |  | 60 coins | Dropped by The Storm Griffin; Dropped by monsters in The Shattered Highlands
Dread Crystal | Epic |  | 2,500 coins | Dropped by The Ash Colossus; Dropped by The Astral Sentinel

The Haunted Moors drop Ectoplasm and the Shattered Highlands drop Gale Essence. The Dread Crystal drops glowing on the ground, with a chime, and is the same in every region. All essences sell for 60 coins and a Dread Crystal for 2,500.
Forests and taiga. 3 skulls, +15 levels. Fog dark red, density 0.3.

A rot spreads from something buried deep. The grass becomes blightgrass, trees turn into dead pale oak, dirt becomes coarse dirt, flowers become wither roses. Scattered blight crystals, bone spikes, soul soil and the odd skull.
Monsters: Blighted Dead (armoured zombies), Blight Archers, Gravecallers, Hollow Wisps, Blight Witches. Drops: Blight Essence. Boss: The Blight Lord.
Savanna, badlands and desert. 4 skulls, +18 levels. Fog ash grey, density 0.35.
Burnt flat by a fire that never went out. Ashen soil replaces sand and grass, trunks are stripped and bare, and the ground is dotted with magma patches, basalt pillars and smooth basalt.
Monsters: Ember Imps, Ash Walkers (husks), Cinder Wraiths (blazes), Charred Revenants (wither skeletons). Drops: Cinder Essence. Boss: The Ash Colossus.
Snowy biomes, ice spikes, groves. 4 skulls, +18 levels. Fog white, density 0.3.

Fifteen Italian brainrot creatures wander the survival world. Catch them all for your album and hear each one say its name.

Brainrots are fifteen silly creatures that turn up on the surface of the survival world: Tung Tung Tung Sahur with his bat, Tralalero Tralala in his sneakers, Bombardiro Crocodilo circling overhead, and twelve more. Walk up to one and it shouts its own name. Right-click it to catch it, and it goes into your album, where you can look at it and hear it again whenever you like.

They appear on the surface of the survival world, 20 to 44 blocks from you, never in Skyhaven, caves or other dimensions.
They're not common: about one every five or six minutes while you're out exploring, and only one near you at a time. They don't stay long either: after 6 minutes (or once you go far away) a brainrot vanishes in a puff.
Some like certain places (see the table) and are much more common there: beach brainrots on beaches, desert ones in deserts. Cappuccino Assassino mostly comes out at night, and La Vaca Saturno Saturnita comes out only at night.
When one is within 10 blocks it says its name, with music notes over its head, so listen out.

They move in their own ways: most walk, some hop, Ballerina Cappuccina spins, La Vaca Saturno Saturnita floats just off the ground, and the two fliers (Bombardiro Crocodilo and Bombombini Gusini) circle high above you. Fliers swoop down to head height every half a minute or so (sooner while you're close) and fly slowly for a few seconds: that's when you catch them.
Right-click a brainrot to catch it. It shouts its name one last time and vanishes in a puff, and you get coins:

Catching one for the first time shows NEW BRAINROT! on your screen. Brainrots can't be hurt (hitting one just makes it jump), and whoever right-clicks first gets it. Catch all fifteen and you're a Brainrot Master: the whole server hears about it.

When anyone catches a brainrot, a card slides in at the top left for everyone on the server: the catcher and the brainrot side by side, both turning in 3D, who caught what (NEW BRAINROT! if it was their first of that kind, or how many they have now) and its rarity. The brainrot shouts its name for everyone else too. If several come at once, they queue up.
Move or resize the card in the HUD editor ("Brainrot catches"). In Settings → Brainrots, choose Card and voice, Card only or Off.
The top three brainrot collectors stand on a podium in Skyhaven, on the lawn just south-east of spawn (around 12, 25), facing the plaza:

Statues of them with their skins, 1st on the gold pedestal in the middle, 2nd on silver to its left and 3rd on copper to its right. They turn their heads to watch you walk past, and #1 sparkles.
A plate on each pedestal shows their name, how many of the fifteen they've found, how many catches they've made in all, and how many kinds of each rarity they have, coloured by rarity.
The ranking is by kinds found, then total catches, then whoever got there first. It updates as people catch, and a new #1 gets a burst of colour.
Players who caught brainrots before the leaderboard existed are added the next time they join.
Press J (or open the K menu and pick Brainrots) to open your album.

A card for each brainrot, coloured by rarity. Ones you've caught show their 3D model (it turns to follow your mouse) and how many times you've caught it. Ones you haven't are a ? with their rarity.
Click a card to see it up close on the right, with its description, where it's found and when you first caught it. Clicking a caught one plays its voice, and ▶ Hear it plays it again.
The bar at the top shows how many of the fifteen you have.
Your album is saved with your character and stays with you when you die. J can be changed in Controls, under SkyRPG.

The shrine at the centre of every danger region, its six bosses and their moves, Heart Sigils and what the bosses drop.

Every danger region has a heart at its centre: a ruined shrine with an altar. A boss sleeps there. You can wake it with a Heart Sigil, or wait for a Blood Moon to wake it for you. Defeating one pays out huge coin rewards, a trophy, essences, Blood Shards and a good chance of a Dread Crystal.
The shrine is built when the region's chunks generate (only in newly generated chunks) and reaches 8 blocks from the centre:

A round platform of the region's own stone, with a checkerboard of lighter blocks at the middle.
A low, ruined wall around the edge, open at the four ways in.
Four pillars, five blocks high, each topped with a light.
An altar in the middle: a 3x3 step, a plinth and the heart block on top.
Anything above the platform is cleared, so trees and slopes do not bury it. The boss appears 3.5 blocks east of the altar.

The red-moon nights that make the Overworld deadlier and richer, with hordes, double drops, Blood Shards and awakened region hearts.

Now and then the moon rises red over the Overworld. Everything hostile gets stronger, hordes hunt you, and the bosses at the centre of every danger region wake up. It is risky, but kills drop twice as much, and it is the only source of Blood Shards, the material for Heart Sigils and the Moonblood Charm.

At dusk each night (when the day clock reaches 13,000) the game rolls for a Blood Moon in the Overworld. The chance is 12%.
It never happens two nights in a row, and it is guaranteed on the twelfth night without one.
There must be at least one non-spectator player in the Overworld for it to be rolled.
It lasts from dusk to dawn, ending at time 23,000. Sleeping through the night ends it too.
It is saved with the world, so restarting the server does not end it.

At sunset you get a red notice ("The moon rises red...") and a BLOOD MOON banner, with a low horn. The sky, the clouds and the fog turn red over about ten seconds, the moon is full, and a Blood Moon timer appears on your HUD showing how long is left.

Region monsters spawn every 1.5 seconds instead of every 3, with twice the usual cap.
Region drops are rolled twice.
Region monsters are Bloodbound too, and vanish at dawn.

When any player comes within 64 blocks of the heart, the boss wakes at the altar, and everyone within 160 blocks hears about it. Each heart wakes once per moon, and the waypoint clears when you get close.
See Region Hearts for the bosses.
A Blood Moon is the cheapest way to fight a region boss, because you do not need a Heart Sigil. It is also a way to collect enough Blood Shards to craft sigils for later.

Crates drop from monsters in the survival world. Open one with its key and a long reel of prizes spins past a gold marker, ticking as it goes, slows down and stops on what you win, from blue (common) up to the gold ★ prizes. The rarer tiers get a bigger fanfare, and Cursed and better prizes are announced to everyone on the server. Gold ★ prizes stay hidden on the reel as ★ Rare Special Item until one lands.

The four underground layers of the Overworld, with their blocks, ores, monsters, levels and drops, plus Abandoned Mine Camps and Runeforged armour.

The deeper you dig, the stranger the caves get. Underground, the Overworld is split into four layers, each with its own look, monsters, level bonus and drops. Going down is how you find the best ores, and the layers are where the Mining skill, Delving and Combat meet.
A layer applies only in Overworld caves, within its height band, and out of sight of the sky. Heights run from the lowest block of the band, so Glimmer Caverns covers y 0 to 39.
Glimmer Caverns | y 0 to 40 | 1 skull | +4 | Glimmerstone, calcite, Glimmer Clusters, glow lichen | Glimmer Crawlers, Lost Miners, cave spiders | Glimmer Geode
Fungal Depths | y -20 to 0 | 2 skulls | +7 | Mycelium and moss, glowcaps, giant mushrooms, Spore Puffballs | Sporelings, Spore Shamblers, cave spiders | Glowcap Spores
Dwarven Halls | y -40 to -20 | 3 skulls | +10 | Deepslate brick and tile, broken pillars, chains and lanterns, runestones | Dwarven Constructs, Lost Miners, skeletons | Dwarven Cog
Magma Rifts | y -64 to -40 | 4 skulls | +14 | Basalt, blackstone, magma, lava pools | Fire Beetles, magma cubes, blazes | Rift Ember
The Dwarven Halls layer is the cave style. The Dwarven Halls dungeon is a separate ruined city found under mountains, hills and forests. See Dwarven Halls.

The land. Cave surfaces (stone, deepslate, tuff, granite, diorite, andesite, dirt and gravel next to cave air) are restyled as chunks generate, about 60 to 75% of them depending on the layer. Edges between layers blur by about 3 blocks, so layers bleed together. Nothing within 3 blocks of the surface changes, water-filled caves stay as they were, and vanilla lush caves, dripstone caves and the deep dark are left alone. Chunks made before the update keep their old look, but the monsters, levels and drops still apply.
Levels. A layer's bonus stacks with the usual underground levels (+5 below y 0, +10 below y -32). In the Magma Rifts that is +10 and +14, so +24 on top of the surface level for that distance.
Spawns. Every 3 seconds, near each survival player in a layer, a group spawns 10 to 24 blocks away on solid ground in the dark (block light of at most 7 to 9, depending on the layer), up to 6 to 8 layer monsters within 40 blocks. They can despawn normally.
Titles. Entering a layer shows its name, skulls and level bonus. You are only counted as in a new layer once you are 2 blocks past the edge, and the same layer's title is not repeated for a minute.
Drops. Monsters killed by a player inside roll the layer's drop: Glimmer Geode 3%, Glowcap Spores 30% (1 to 2), Dwarven Cog 25%, Rift Ember 25% (1 to 2).

Obsidian Spires | Tall obsidian and crying obsidian pillars, blackstone flats, glowing void cracks | Deep purple | Endermen, wither skeletons, ghasts, magma cubes | Crying obsidian, rich Hellforged veins
Striders live in all three, as in the rest of the Nether.
A hunched giant skeleton of the Bone Sea. It is slow, tough (110 base health, heavy knockback resistance) and fire-immune, and it strides over soul sand without sinking in.

Club swing: it raises its femur club, then smashes the ground in front of it. Step aside during the wind-up.
Bone quake: about every 10 seconds, when you are within 5 blocks, it rears up for a second with a ring of soul fire on the ground, then stomps. Everyone within 4 blocks is damaged, thrown up and slowed.
Drops: bones, sometimes bone blocks and soul soil, and when a player kills one there is a 12% chance of a Hellforged Scrap.
Hellforged Ore generates in Nether stone (netherrack, blackstone, basalt) at y 10 to 117 and needs a Tier 5 pickaxe.
Anywhere in the Nether | Small veins, 2 per chunk
Ember Forest, Bone Sea, Obsidian Spires | Richer veins, 8 per chunk
Obsidian Spires only | Big veins of 10, 3 per chunk
Mining it drops Hellforged Scrap. Smelt the scrap in a blast furnace (10 seconds) to make a Hellforged Ingot. Scrap sells for 28 coins and an ingot for 32.

The Hellforged Pickaxe (Tier VI, Mining level 40) is upgraded from the Emberheart Pickaxe with 24 Hellforged Ingots and 8 Emberite Ingots. It has 260 Mining Speed and 100 Mining Fortune, smelts what you mine automatically, and its right-click Hellfire Vein makes every ore you mine also break a touching ore of the same kind for 15 seconds.
The Hellforged armour set is crafted in the dungeon category with Delving level 30:
Hellforged Warplate | 20 | 10 | 128 Health, 112 Defense, 34 Strength, plus a Tyrant's Core
The full set grants Forged in Fire: fire and lava cannot hurt you or set you alight, you see clearly through lava, and you gain +60 Defense and +40 Strength.

A blackstone fortress on the Nether's lava sea, built over lava bridges and into cliffs. It is a two-floor dungeon at level 48 with blazes, wither skeletons, Ember Imps and piglin brutes, lava traps and per-player chests. See Infernal Citadel for the full walk-through.

Champion: The Infernal Knight (level 50, 14,000 health), a giant wither skeleton in blackened plate. It drops the Citadel Key.
Boss: The Magma Tyrant (level 52, 36,000 health).
Reset: the dungeon resets three in-game days after it is used up, when nobody is nearby.
A huge molten-rock titan with a crown of fire. Each extra player adds 60% to its health. The moves repeat on timers:
Magma Cubes and Ember Imps summon (2 and 3, up to 6) | 23.5 s | Below 66%
Pull towards the heart (radius 16) | 19 s | Below 66%
Molten floor (14 spots, radius 5) | 12 s | Below 33%
Below 33% it also enrages: faster and harder-hitting.

Rewards: 36,000 to 48,000 coins each, and 70,000 coins, 20,000 Combat XP and 16,000 Delving XP on a first clear. Loot includes a Tyrant's Core (25% for a second), a Citadel Key, 8 to 14 Hellforged Scrap, 2 to 4 Hellforged Ingots, 2 to 4 Netherite Scrap and 5 to 9 Emberite Ingots, plus a Reward Chest. The Tyrant's Core sells for 6,200 coins.
The Magmaline Rod lets you fish in lava in the Nether. Its bobber floats on lava, cannot burn, and bites like normal, and your catch goes straight to your inventory.
Crafting: a Leviathan Rod, 8 Hellforged Ingots and a Tyrant's Core, at Fishing level 40. It has 90 Fishing Speed, 85 Fishing Fortune and 7 Sea Creature Chance, with a 14% chance of a double catch.
On top of that, about 1 in 250 lava catches is a Molten Pearl (sells for 2,500).
Lava sea creatures can come up instead: Magma Slugs (level 40, common), Flame Serpents (level 42, rare) and very rarely the Cinder Leviathan (level 45, with a boss bar). See Fishing.
Stock up on Hellforged ingots before you start: the Hellforged set gives lava immunity, which is useful when you are standing on a lava lake with a fishing rod.

The three new outer-End biomes, Starstone and Astral Crystals, the Astral Observatory dungeon, and where the Ender Wyrm is fought.

After the dragon, the outer End still has plenty to offer. Three new biomes change the outer islands, a new ore-like crystal gives Astral Shards, and a dungeon, the Astral Observatory, hides the End's own boss. Mobs in the End start at level 40, the highest base level in the game.
The new biomes only appear in newly generated outer-End chunks. The main island, and any outer islands you have already visited, are not changed.

Each new biome replaces some of a vanilla biome's area, so you will still see ordinary End highlands, midlands and small islands among them. Find them with /locate biome skyrpg_world:void_gardens (or shattered_isles, astral_fields).
Void Gardens | End Highlands | about 44% | Endermen
Shattered Isles | Small outer islands | about 44% | Endermen, endermites
Astral Fields | End Midlands (under the highlands and the Void Gardens) | about 47% | Endermen, endermites

Purple void trees with a purpur trunk and branches and a canopy of glowing Void Cap. Patches of violet Void Bloom cover the ground (it glows at light 8), alongside vanilla chorus plants. The sky and fog are a deep violet.

Small outer islands as in vanilla, plus floating rubble islets of end stone, end stone bricks, purpur and amethyst at heights 40 to 100, with amethyst clusters and loose stepping stones. They are linked by gaps that you must bridge or jump.

End stone with stars in the ground. About one surface block in six becomes Starstone, and about one column in ninety grows an Astral Crystal, often with a second beside it. The sky and fog are deep blue.
Starstone | End stone with glowing specks (light 6). A building block.
Astral Crystal | A glowing crystal cluster (light 11). Break it with a pickaxe for 2 to 4 Astral Shards. Silk Touch keeps the block.
Astral Shard | A rare material full of cold starlight. It goes into the Void Sigil that summons the Ender Wyrm (16 for three Sigils; see Ender Wyrm) and into the Voidreaver sword.
Void Cap | The glowing canopy block of void trees.
Astral Fields give the easiest Astral Shards: wander the fields with a pickaxe and break every crystal you see. The Star Warden also drops 8 to 14 shards on each kill.

A purpur and glass observatory on stilts, found on the outer islands in all five of the biomes above (the vanilla highlands and midlands too). Inside are star-map halls, archives and telescope rooms. It is a level 64 dungeon in two floors: the Lower Halls, then a 20-block climb up to the Star Deck. See Astral Observatory for the whole dungeon.
The Astral Sentinel (champion, level 62) | 24,000 | Blinks, slams, looses five star-bolts, wraps itself in a ward below 50%, and summons Void Mites.

The Star Warden (boss, level 64) | 60,000 | Blinks, fires volleys of starlight and slams. Below 66% it pulls players in and summons Acolytes and Void Mites. Below 50% it wards, and below 33% it sends shockwaves and enrages.
The Star Warden drops 1 to 2 Star Warden's Core (sells for 11,000 coins), an Observatory Key for the vault behind his dome, and 8 to 14 Astral Shards. It also leaves a Reward Chest.

No new monsters live in the End biomes yet: it is vanilla endermen and endermites at higher levels.
The Void Stalker only exists as a slayer boss, not as a wandering mob.
The End does not have its own waystone, except at the Observatory entrance. See Waystones and Travel.

The End's last boss, the Ender Wyrm, is called with a Void Sigil used in the End after the Ender Dragon is dead. A Sigil is crafted at the Artisan Bench from Astral Shards and one of each dungeon trophy (the Star Warden's Core is the End's). The fight pays Wyrm Scales and Void Hearts to everyone who took part, for the Wyrmscale armour and the Voidreaver sword. See Ender Wyrm.
